lessons.plain: This objective is about the standard tools for checking whether data shows something real, and for scoring how good a model is. Some tools test a claim, such as whether two groups really differ or whether two categories are linked, rather than the gap being luck. Others grade predictions: how close a model's number guesses come to the truth, or how well a yes/no model catches what it should without crying wolf. Think of a doctor. One set of tools asks whether a new drug actually works. The other asks how often a screening test catches sick patients and how often it wrongly alarms healthy ones.
lessons.guessPrompt: A spam filter is checked on 1,000 emails, of which 60 are spam. It catches 40 of those 60 spam emails and wrongly flags 10 normal emails. It is correct on 970 of the 1,000 emails, so 97% accurate. Would you call it a good filter, and what number would worry you?
lessons.teach:
Hypothesis testing decides whether a pattern in data is likely real or just chance. You state a null hypothesis, meaning a claim of no difference or no relationship. You compute a test statistic and get a p-value. The p-value is the probability of a result at least this extreme if the null were true. If it falls below a threshold set in advance, called alpha (often 0.05), you reject the null.

Pick the test by data type. A t-test compares the means of a numeric variable between two groups. ANOVA (analysis of variance) compares means across three or more groups at once, which avoids the false alarms you pile up by running many t-tests. A chi-squared test checks whether two categorical variables are related. It compares the observed counts in a table with the counts you would expect if the variables were independent.

Regression models predict numbers. R-squared (R2) is the share of the target's variation the model explains: 1 is perfect, and 0 is no better than always predicting the average. RMSE (root mean squared error) is the typical error size in the target's own units, and it punishes large misses heavily.

Classifiers sort items into classes, here yes or no. A confusion matrix counts their true positives (TP), false positives (FP), false negatives (FN) and true negatives (TN). Precision = TP/(TP+FP), the share of flagged items that were right. Recall = TP/(TP+FN), the share of real positives caught. F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. MCC (Matthews correlation coefficient) uses all four cells and runs from -1 to +1, where 0 means chance level.

Worked example: a fraud model scores TP=40, FP=10, FN=20, TN=930. Precision = 40/50 = 0.80. Recall = 40/60 = 0.67. F1 = 2×0.80×0.67/(0.80+0.67) ≈ 0.73. MCC = (40×930 − 10×20)/√(50×60×940×950) ≈ 0.72.

Common mistake: reporting accuracy alone. Accuracy here is 97%, yet a third of the fraud slipped through, and flagging nothing would still score 94%. In production, the wrong metric lets a model ship that misses the very cases it exists to catch.

questions.prompt: A factory camera system flags circuit boards as defective. On a batch of 500 boards it scores TP=30, FP=20, FN=10, TN=440. Step 1: Precision = TP/(TP+FP) = 30/50 = 0.60. Step 2: Recall = TP/(TP+FN) = 30/40 = 0.75. Step 3: F1 = ? Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
questions.why: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, 2PR/(P+R), which gives 0.90/1.35 ≈ 0.67. The other choices are the simple average, the plain product, and accuracy.

questions.prompt: A logistics company wants to know whether the average delivery time in minutes differs across its four regional warehouses. Which test fits this question best?
choices: ANOVA, because it compares means across three or more groups in one test
A chi-squared test, because the warehouses are categories
R-squared, because it measures how much variation is explained
A t-test, because delivery time is a numeric variable
questions.why: ANOVA compares the means of a numeric variable across three or more groups at once. This avoids the extra false alarms that come from running many separate t-tests.

questions.prompt: A model predicts taxi trip duration in minutes. On test data it reports R2 = 0.85 and RMSE = 6 minutes. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: 85% of the trips were predicted exactly right, and the rest were off by 6%
It explains 85% of trip-time variation, and a typical error is about 6 minutes, with big misses weighted heavily
RMSE of 6 means the model is 6 times better than predicting the average
The model's p-value is 0.15, so the null hypothesis is rejected
questions.why: R2 is the share of the target's variation the model explains. RMSE is the typical error size in the target's own units (minutes here), and it punishes large misses heavily.

questions.prompt: A clinic tests whether a new appointment-reminder text changes no-show rates. Before looking at the data, the team sets alpha at 0.01. The test returns a p-value of 0.03. What should they conclude?
choices: Lower alpha to 0.001 so the result counts as significant
Do not reject the null hypothesis, because 0.03 is not below the 0.01 threshold
Reject the null hypothesis, because 0.03 is below the usual 0.05
Reject the null hypothesis, because there is a 97% chance the reminder works
questions.why: You reject the null hypothesis only when the p-value falls below the alpha set in advance. Here 0.03 is above 0.01, so the null stands. Switching to 0.05 after seeing the result would defeat the purpose of fixing alpha in advance.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a t-test, ANOVA and a chi-squared test. Then explain why you would report precision, recall, F1 or MCC instead of accuracy for a rare-event classifier, naming one tradeoff between precision and recall.
lessons.modelAnswer: I choose the test by the kind of data and the number of groups. If I'm comparing a numeric average between two groups, I use a t-test. With three or more groups I use ANOVA, because running many t-tests inflates the chance of a false alarm. If both variables are categories, like region and churned-or-not, I use a chi-squared test on the count table. In every case I set alpha in advance and reject the null only if the p-value falls below it. For rare events, accuracy misleads, because predicting 'no' every time can still score very high. Precision tells me how many of my flags are right, and recall tells me how many real cases I caught. F1 balances the two, and MCC uses all four confusion-matrix cells. The tradeoff is that flagging more aggressively raises recall but usually lowers precision, so the right balance depends on whether a miss or a false alarm costs more.
rubricPoints: Matches the test to the data: t-test for two group means, ANOVA for three or more groups, chi-squared for two categorical variables.
Describes the p-value compared against a preset alpha to decide whether to reject the null hypothesis.
Defines precision and recall correctly in terms of false positives and false negatives.
Explains why accuracy misleads on imbalanced data and why F1 or MCC helps.
Names the precision-versus-recall tradeoff and ties it to the cost of errors.

suggested.rationale: The skill tested is picking the right test or metric for a described situation, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios with small hand calculations builds it best, and no current mission or planned engine covers statistics.

lessons.plain: This objective is about describing uncertainty. A probability distribution is a recipe for how likely each possible outcome is: a bell curve for heights, equal odds for a fair die, counts of arrivals per hour. Shape words like skew and heavy tails tell you when data does not behave like a neat bell. Simulation methods let a computer roll the dice thousands of times so you can see the range of possible results. Bayes' rule is a way to update a belief when new evidence arrives, like a weather forecaster revising tomorrow's rain chance after seeing the morning clouds. Together they help you pick the right model of randomness instead of guessing.
lessons.guessPrompt: A disease affects 1 in 100 people. A test catches 90% of sick people but also wrongly flags 5% of healthy people. If someone tests positive, is their chance of being sick closer to 90%, 50%, or 15%?
lessons.teach:
A probability distribution describes how likely each possible value is. The normal distribution is a symmetric bell curve set by its mean (center) and standard deviation (typical spread); it fits values built from many small effects, like heights. The uniform distribution makes every value in a range equally likely, like a fair die. The binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent yes/no trials with the same success chance, like defective parts in a batch of 20. The Poisson distribution counts events in a fixed interval when they arrive independently at an average rate, like tickets per hour; its mean equals its variance.

Skewness measures lopsidedness: right-skewed data has a long tail of large values, pulling the mean above the median. Kurtosis measures tail heaviness: high kurtosis means more extreme outliers than a normal curve predicts. Heteroskedasticity means a model's error spread changes with the input, such as spending errors growing with income. It breaks regression's constant-variance assumption, making confidence intervals untrustworthy.

Monte Carlo simulation estimates an answer by drawing many random samples from assumed distributions and summarizing the results. Bootstrapping resamples your own data with replacement many times, recomputing a statistic each time to see how much it varies, without assuming a distribution.

Bayes' rule updates a prior belief with evidence: P(A given B) = P(B given A) × P(A) / P(B). Worked example with 10,000 people, 1% sick, 90% detection, 5% false positives: 100 are sick and 90 test positive; 9,900 are healthy and 495 test positive. That is 585 positives, so P(sick given positive) = 90/585, about 15%.

The common mistake is confusing P(positive given sick), 90%, with P(sick given positive), 15%, by ignoring the base rate. In a running fraud or alerting system, this is why most alerts on rare events are false alarms. The exam rewards matching tool to situation: counts per interval suggest Poisson, fixed trials suggest binomial, and uncertainty about one sample's statistic suggests bootstrapping.

questions.prompt: A company's email filter is tested on 20,000 messages. 2% are real phishing emails, the filter flags 95% of phishing emails, and it wrongly flags 3% of legitimate emails. The goal is to find P(phishing given flagged) with Bayes' rule, counting people-style. Step 1: phishing emails = 2% of 20,000 = 400. Step 2: phishing emails flagged = 95% of 400 = 380. Step 3: legitimate emails = 20,000 - 400 = 19,600. Step 4: ??? Step 5: total flagged = 380 + legitimate flagged = 968. Step 6: P(phishing given flagged) = 380 / 968, about 39%. Which choice correctly fills in Step 4?
choices: Legitimate emails flagged = 95% of 19,600 = 18,620
Legitimate emails flagged = 3% of 20,000 = 600
Legitimate emails flagged = 3% of 19,600 = 588
Legitimate emails flagged = 5% of 400 = 20
questions.why: The 3% false-flag rate applies only to the 19,600 legitimate emails, giving 588, which matches the 968 total in Step 5.

questions.prompt: A data center team records how many unplanned power interruptions happen each month. The interruptions occur independently at a fairly steady average rate. Which distribution best fits the monthly count?
choices: Binomial, because each month is a yes/no trial
Uniform, because every count from zero upward is equally likely
Poisson, because it counts independent events in a fixed interval at an average rate
Normal, because counts usually form a bell curve
questions.why: Counts of independent events per fixed interval at an average rate are the defining case for the Poisson distribution, not fixed-trial binomial counts.

questions.prompt: An analyst fits a regression predicting delivery time from delivery distance. The errors are small for short trips but spread out much more widely for long trips. What does this pattern indicate?
choices: High kurtosis, so the distances contain too many extreme outliers
Right skewness, so the mean delivery time sits below the median
A uniform error distribution, so every error size is equally likely
Heteroskedasticity, so the model's confidence intervals cannot be trusted
questions.why: Error spread that changes with the input is heteroskedasticity, which breaks regression's constant-variance assumption and makes confidence intervals untrustworthy.

questions.prompt: A clinic has one sample of 60 patient wait times and wants to know how much the median wait might vary from sample to sample, without assuming any particular distribution. Which approach fits best?
choices: Fitting a Poisson distribution, because wait times are counts per hour
Bayes' rule, updating a prior belief about the median with the evidence
Monte Carlo simulation drawing samples from an assumed normal distribution
Bootstrapping: resample the 60 times with replacement and recompute the median
questions.why: Bootstrapping resamples your own data with replacement to measure how a statistic varies, with no distribution assumed, whereas Monte Carlo draws from assumed distributions.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between Monte Carlo simulation and bootstrapping, and use Bayes' rule to show why a highly accurate detector can still produce mostly false alarms. Name one limit of each simulation method.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both methods use repeated random draws, but the source differs. Monte Carlo draws from distributions we assume, for example Poisson arrivals and normal service times, and runs the scenario thousands of times to see the spread of outcomes. Its limit is that the results are only as good as those assumptions. Bootstrapping draws with replacement from the data we actually collected and recomputes a statistic each time to estimate its uncertainty. Its limit is that it cannot invent behavior missing from a small or biased sample. For alarms, Bayes' rule says P(fraud given alert) depends on the base rate. If fraud is 1% of cases, a detector that catches 90% with a 5% false-positive rate yields only about 15% true alerts, because there are so many more legitimate cases to misflag. Thresholds must account for the prior.
rubricPoints: Monte Carlo samples from assumed distributions, while bootstrapping resamples the observed data with replacement.
States a limit: Monte Carlo depends on its assumptions, and bootstrapping depends on how representative the sample is.
Bayes' rule combines a prior or base rate with the evidence likelihood.
Distinguishes P(evidence given condition) from P(condition given evidence).
Explains that rare events lead to many false positives even with an accurate detector.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers probability, and the core exam skill is reasoning through scenarios to choose the right distribution, resampling method, or Bayesian update.

lessons.plain: Linear algebra is the math of tables of numbers (matrices) and lists of numbers (vectors). Calculus is the math of how one quantity changes when another changes. Data science leans on both. A dataset is a matrix: each row a record, each column a feature. Distances between rows tell you which records look alike. Derivatives tell a model which way to nudge its settings to make fewer errors. Think of hiking in fog. Linear algebra is your map of where everything sits. Calculus is feeling the slope under your feet so you know which step goes downhill.
lessons.guessPrompt: Shopper A bought 2 apples and 4 pears. Shopper B bought 20 apples and 40 pears. Do they have similar tastes or different ones? What does your answer depend on?
lessons.teach:
A matrix is a grid of numbers. A vector is a single row or column of numbers. Matrix multiplication combines rows of the first matrix with columns of the second, so the inner sizes must match. Order matters: AB usually differs from BA. The transpose flips rows into columns.

Rank is the number of linearly independent rows or columns, meaning those that cannot be built from the others. If a feature equals another feature times two, the data matrix loses rank. Regression then has no single best answer and its coefficients become unstable. This problem is called multicollinearity.

For a square matrix A, an eigenvector v is a direction that A only stretches, so Av = λv. The stretch factor λ is the eigenvalue. In PCA (principal component analysis, a way to compress many features into a few), the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix measure how much variance each new direction captures. An eigenvalue near zero signals a redundant direction.

Distance metrics compare two vectors. Take P = (1,2) and Q = (4,6). The differences are 3 and 4.
Euclidean (straight line): √(9+16) = 5.
Manhattan (grid steps, sum of absolute differences): 3+4 = 7.
Cosine similarity looks at angle, not length. It is the dot product divided by both lengths: (4+12)/(√5·√52) ≈ 0.99. That means nearly the same direction.

A partial derivative measures how an output changes when one input moves and the others are held fixed. The gradient collects all the partial derivatives. The chain rule handles nested functions: the rate of change of f(g(x)) is f′(g(x))·g′(x). For a loss L = (wx − y)², the inner part is u = wx − y. So ∂L/∂w = 2u·x. Backpropagation is the chain rule applied layer by layer through a neural network.

A common mistake is using Euclidean or Manhattan distance on unscaled features. A salary column in thousands then swamps an age column, and k-nearest-neighbours or clustering effectively ignores age. Standardize features first. For text or count data, where overall size is not the point, prefer cosine.

questions.prompt:
A warehouse tracks two delivery robots by position in three dimensions (aisle, shelf, height). Robot A is at (2, 0, 3) and Robot B is at (5, 4, 15). The team wants the Euclidean (straight-line) distance between them.
Step 1: Subtract coordinate by coordinate. The differences are 3, 4 and 12.
Step 2: Square each difference: 9, 16 and 144.
Step 3: ???
What is the result of Step 3, the Euclidean distance?
choices: 19, the sum of the absolute differences 3 + 4 + 12
13, the square root of 9 + 16 + 144
5, the square root of 9 + 16, using only the first two coordinates
169, the sum of the squared differences 9 + 16 + 144
questions.why: Euclidean distance adds the squared differences across every coordinate and then takes the square root, so √(9 + 16 + 144) = √169 = 13.

questions.prompt: A clinic builds a regression model, a model that predicts a number from input features, to predict blood pressure. Its features are patient height in centimetres, the same height converted to inches (centimetres divided by 2.54), and weight. What does this do to the data matrix and the model?
choices: The matrix can no longer be transposed, so the regression cannot be fitted at all
The matrix keeps full rank because the two height columns hold different numbers, so the model is unaffected
The matrix loses rank because one height column can be built from the other, so the regression has no single best answer and its coefficients become unstable
The matrix gains an extra eigenvalue, which makes the regression more accurate
questions.why: Rank counts the columns that cannot be built from the others. Inches is just centimetres times a constant, so rank drops. This is multicollinearity, which makes the regression coefficients unstable.

questions.prompt: A news site represents articles as word-count vectors, lists of how often each word appears. A short article has counts (2, 4) for the words 'match' and 'goal'. A long article has counts (20, 40). The team wants to know whether the two articles cover the same topic, regardless of length. Which measure fits, and what does it show?
choices: Euclidean distance after standardizing, which will always equal zero for any two articles
Euclidean distance, which is about 40, so the topics are very different
Manhattan distance, which is 54, so the topics are very different
Cosine similarity, which is 1 because the vectors point in exactly the same direction, so the topics match
questions.why: Cosine similarity compares only the angle between vectors and ignores their length. (20, 40) is exactly 10 times (2, 4), so the angle is zero and the similarity is 1.

questions.prompt: An analyst runs PCA (principal component analysis, which compresses many features into a few new directions) on sensor data from a factory. The eigenvalues of the covariance matrix come out as 8.0, 1.5 and 0.002. What does the eigenvalue of 0.002 most likely tell the analyst?
choices: Its direction captures the most variance because small eigenvalues mean tight, reliable data
The sensors must be measured with cosine similarity instead of Euclidean distance
The covariance matrix was multiplied in the wrong order, so the result is invalid
Its direction captures almost no variance, so it is redundant and can likely be dropped
questions.why: In PCA each eigenvalue measures how much variance its direction captures. A value near zero signals a redundant direction that adds little information.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would pick cosine similarity over Euclidean distance. Then explain why a low-rank feature matrix or a near-zero eigenvalue is a warning sign. Name one limit or tradeoff of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Euclidean distance measures the straight-line gap between two records, so it is sensitive to magnitude. Two documents on the same topic, one ten times longer, look far apart under Euclidean distance. Cosine similarity compares only the angle between the vectors. It would call them similar, which is why it suits text and count data. The tradeoff is that cosine throws away size, so when magnitude matters, such as spend amounts, you lose real information. With either distance, unscaled features let large-unit columns dominate, so you standardize first. Rank is the number of independent columns. If it is lower than the column count, some features are combinations of others. Regression coefficients then become unstable or undefined. A near-zero eigenvalue of the covariance matrix flags the same redundancy. PCA can drop that direction, but the new components are harder to interpret than the original features.
rubricPoints: Euclidean distance depends on magnitude, while cosine similarity compares only direction or angle.
Cosine suits text or count data but discards size information.
Features should be scaled before using distance-based methods.
Rank is the number of independent columns, and low rank means redundant features and unstable regression.
Eigenvalues measure variance along directions, and near-zero values flag redundancy, as used in PCA.
The chain rule lets gradients pass through nested functions, which is the basis of backpropagation.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right metric or spotting rank and gradient issues in a scenario, and no current mission or planned engine exercises this math, so reasoning through exam-style situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: These are three families of tools for data that unfolds over time. Each answers a different question. Time series models ask what comes next, by learning from a measurement's own past, like predicting tomorrow's website traffic from recent days. Survival analysis asks how long until something happens, such as a customer cancelling, even when some customers have not cancelled yet. Causal inference asks whether a change actually caused a result, like whether a new checkout page really raised sales or whether sales would have risen anyway. Think of a weather forecaster, an insurance actuary and a detective: they share the same calendar but do different jobs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A subscription company wants to know how long customers typically stay, but half of its customers are still subscribed today. What goes wrong if you simply leave those still-subscribed customers out of the average?
lessons.teach:
A time series is one variable measured at regular intervals, and time series analysis models it from its own history. An autoregressive model, AR(p), predicts today's value from the previous p values. A moving-average model, MA(q), predicts it from the previous q forecast errors, meaning the gaps between what the model predicted and what actually happened. ARIMA(p,d,q) combines both and adds the I, for integrated. That step differences the series d times, subtracting each value from the one after it, to remove trend. The goal is a stationary series, one whose mean and variance stay stable over time. AR and MA both assume stationarity, which is why differencing matters.

Survival analysis models the time until an event, such as churn or a machine failing. Its key idea is censoring. Some subjects have not had the event when observation stops, so you only know their time is at least that long. A survival curve, often estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method, shows the share of subjects still event-free at each point in time. The hazard is the instant risk of the event at a given moment for subjects still at risk.

Causal inference estimates whether X causes Y, not just whether the two move together. A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a diagram of one-way arrows, with no loops, showing assumed cause-and-effect paths. It helps you spot confounders, which are variables that drive both X and Y. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) assigns treatment by chance, so confounders balance out across groups. An A/B test is an RCT on a product, comparing version A with version B. When you cannot randomize, difference-in-differences (DiD) compares a treated group's change over time with an untreated group's change. It assumes parallel trends, meaning both groups would have moved alike without the treatment.

Worked example: a promotion runs only in Store A. Store A's weekly sales go from 100 to 130, and Store B's go from 100 to 110. Store A changed by 30 and Store B by 10. The DiD estimate is 30 minus 10, or 20 units caused by the promotion. The 10 is shared background drift.

Common mistake: dropping censored customers, or treating their last observed date as a churn date. Both errors make survival times look shorter than they are. A live retention dashboard built that way would overstate how fast customers leave.

questions.prompt: A school district starts a tutoring program in its North schools only. Average test scores in North go from 60 to 72 over the year. In South, which had no tutoring, scores go from 62 to 66. An analyst uses difference-in-differences (DiD), which compares the treated group's change over time with the untreated group's change. Step 1: North's change is 72 minus 60, or 12 points. Step 2: South's change is 66 minus 62, or 4 points. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The analyst notes that this estimate only holds if both regions would have moved alike without tutoring (parallel trends). What is Step 3?
choices: The estimate is 12 minus 4, or 8 points caused by tutoring, with the 4 treated as shared background drift.
The estimate is 12 plus 4, or 16 points, because both regions improved during the year.
The estimate is 6 points, because North ended at 72 and South ended at 66.
The estimate is 12 points, because North's own change already shows the full effect of tutoring.
questions.why: DiD subtracts the untreated group's change (4) from the treated group's change (12), which removes the background drift both groups share and leaves 8 points attributed to tutoring.

questions.prompt: A gym studies how long members stay before cancelling. The study stops collecting data after 14 months. One member joined at the start and is still active when the study ends. In survival analysis, which models the time until an event, how should this member be handled?
choices: Treat the member as cancelling at 14 months, since that is the last date on record.
Keep the member as censored: their time to cancelling is known to be at least 14 months.
Drop the member from the data, since their cancellation date is unknown.
Give the member the average cancellation time of everyone who did cancel.
questions.why: A subject who has not had the event when observation stops is censored, meaning you only know their time is at least that long; dropping them or using the last date as the event both make survival times look shorter.

questions.prompt: An airline wants to forecast monthly ticket sales, which have climbed steadily for five years. The analyst plans an ARIMA(p,d,q) model, which combines autoregressive (past values) and moving-average (past forecast errors) parts. Why should the d value be at least 1 here?
choices: d sets how many past monthly values the model uses to predict the next month.
d sets how many past forecast errors the model uses, and a long trend needs more of them.
d differences the series to remove the upward trend, giving the stable mean that AR and MA assume.
d controls how many future months the model forecasts at once.
questions.why: The I in ARIMA differences the series d times to remove trend so the series becomes stationary, meaning its mean and variance stay stable, which both the AR and MA parts assume.

questions.prompt: A city introduces a congestion charge in its east side only and compares traffic on the east side with traffic on the west side, before and after the charge, using difference-in-differences. Later the analyst finds that west-side traffic had already been falling much faster than east-side traffic for years before the charge. What does this most directly threaten?
choices: The censoring assumption, so some drivers must be treated as still at risk.
The randomization of the trial, so confounders are balanced and the result still holds.
The parallel trends assumption, so the DiD estimate may wrongly credit or blame the charge.
The stationarity assumption, so the analyst must difference the traffic data first.
questions.why: DiD assumes both groups would have moved alike without the treatment; if the untreated group was already on a different path, the difference in changes mixes that gap with the true effect.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a time series model, survival analysis and a causal method like DiD or an A/B test for a business question. Name one assumption or limit of the method you would pick most often.
lessons.modelAnswer: Start with the question. If it is about forecasting the next values of one measurement, like daily orders, I use a time series model. AR uses past values, MA uses past forecast errors, and ARIMA adds differencing to remove trend, because those models need a stationary series. If the question is how long until an event, like churn, I use survival analysis. It handles censoring, which covers customers who haven't churned yet, so their data isn't thrown away or mislabeled. If the question is whether a change caused an outcome, I need causal inference. The best option is a randomized trial such as an A/B test, because randomization balances confounders. If I can't randomize, I use difference-in-differences. Its limit is the parallel-trends assumption: if the two groups were already drifting apart, the estimate is biased. A DAG helps me check which confounders I must account for.
rubricPoints: Matches each method to its question type: forecasting, time-to-event, or cause and effect.
Explains that AR uses past values, MA uses past errors, and ARIMA adds differencing for stationarity.
Explains censoring and why survival analysis must keep censored subjects.
Explains that randomization in an RCT or A/B test balances confounders.
Describes difference-in-differences and its parallel-trends assumption.
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff of the chosen method.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right temporal or causal method for a described situation, which is best practised by reasoning through scenarios, and no current mission or planned engine covers statistical modeling.

lessons.plain: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the first look you take at a dataset before building any model. You count, summarize, and draw simple charts to see what is really there. Univariate analysis studies one column at a time: its typical value, its spread, its shape, and its odd values. Multivariate analysis studies how two or more columns move together. Each chart answers one kind of question, so the skill is matching the chart to the data type and the question. It is like a doctor's checkup before any treatment: you measure first, so later decisions rest on facts instead of guesses.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have two columns, house size in square meters and sale price, both plain numbers. If you wanted to see at a glance whether bigger houses tend to sell for more, what kind of picture would you draw?
lessons.teach:
Exploratory data analysis (EDA) means summarizing and plotting data to understand it before modeling. It works because charts expose patterns, such as skew, outliers, and relationships, that a table of numbers hides.

Univariate analysis examines one variable. For a numeric variable you look at its center (mean or median), its spread, its shape, and its outliers, meaning values far from the rest. A box-and-whisker plot (box plot) shows this compactly. The line inside the box is the median. The box covers the interquartile range (IQR), which is the middle 50% of values, from the 25th to the 75th percentile. The whiskers usually reach up to 1.5 times the IQR beyond the box, and dots past the whiskers are flagged outliers. Placing box plots side by side compares one numeric variable across categories.

A Q-Q plot (quantile-quantile plot) checks whether a variable follows a reference distribution, usually the normal bell curve. Quantiles are the cut points that split sorted data into equal-sized groups. The plot matches the data's quantiles against the reference's quantiles. Points on a straight line mean a good fit. Points bending away at the ends mean skew or heavy tails.

Multivariate analysis examines relationships between variables. A scatter plot puts two numeric variables on the two axes, one dot per row. A heat map is a grid colored by value. Use it for a correlation matrix, which holds the correlation of every pair of numeric columns, or for counts across two categorical variables.

Worked example: a delivery dataset. First, a box plot of delivery minutes shows a median of 30 and several dots above 90. Second, a Q-Q plot against the normal curve bends upward at the top end, which confirms right skew. Third, a scatter plot of distance against minutes shows a rising cloud, so the two are related. Fourth, a correlation heat map shows distance and fuel used at 0.9, so they carry nearly the same information.

A common mistake is putting two categorical columns on a scatter plot. The dots stack on a few grid points and hide the counts, so a count heat map is the right choice. Skipping EDA lets skewed targets, outliers, and redundant features slip silently into the model you build.

questions.prompt: A regional bus company is exploring its ticket data before building a ridership model. Step 1: side-by-side box plots of fare paid (in dollars) for each route type show express routes have a higher median fare than local routes. Step 2: a Q-Q plot of fare paid against the normal curve keeps the points close to a straight line, so fares look roughly normal. Step 3 (missing): the analyst wants to see how two categorical columns, ticket type (single, day pass, monthly) and boarding zone (A, B, C, D), occur together and how many trips fall into each combination. Step 4: a correlation heat map of the numeric columns shows trip length and fare at 0.85, so those two carry much of the same information. Which chart should the analyst use in Step 3?
choices: A Q-Q plot of ticket type against boarding zone
A scatter plot with ticket type on one axis and boarding zone on the other
Side-by-side box plots of boarding zone grouped by ticket type
A heat map of trip counts, with ticket types as rows and zones as columns
questions.why: With two categorical columns, a count heat map shows how many trips fall in each combination, while a scatter plot would stack the dots on a few grid points and hide those counts.

questions.prompt: A box plot of call-center hold times (in seconds) has a box running from 40 to 70, with the median line at 52. Using the usual whisker rule of 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR, the range covered by the middle 50% of values), would a hold time of 130 seconds appear as a flagged outlier dot?
choices: No, because the whiskers reach 1.5 times the median, which allows values up to 148
Yes, because any value above the 75th percentile of 70 is flagged as an outlier
No, because 130 is less than twice the median of 52
Yes, because the IQR is 30, so the upper whisker reaches at most 70 + 45 = 115, and 130 lies beyond it
questions.why: The IQR is 70 - 40 = 30, so the whisker can reach at most 1.5 x 30 = 45 above the box, ending at 115, and 130 falls past that point.

questions.prompt: An analyst at an insurance firm makes a Q-Q plot (quantile-quantile plot) of claim amounts against the normal bell curve. The points sit on a straight line through the middle, but at the far ends they curve sharply away from the line. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: The plot has failed, because Q-Q plots only work on categorical data
Claim amounts are not a good fit to the normal curve; they show skew or heavy tails
Claim amounts are strongly correlated with another variable in the dataset
Claim amounts fit the normal curve well, because most of the points are on the line
questions.why: On a Q-Q plot, points bending away from the straight line at the ends signal skew or heavy tails, which means the data does not closely follow the reference normal distribution.

questions.prompt: A streaming service is preparing features for a churn model. A correlation heat map of its numeric columns shows 'hours watched per month' and 'episodes watched per month' at 0.93. What is the most useful conclusion from this EDA (exploratory data analysis) step?
choices: The two features carry nearly the same information, so keeping both adds redundancy to the model
Both features are outliers and should be removed from the dataset
The two features follow a normal distribution, so no further checks are needed
Hours watched causes customers to watch more episodes, so it should be the target
questions.why: A correlation near 1 on the heat map means the two columns move together almost perfectly, so they hold nearly the same information and can be redundant features if both go into the model.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a box plot, a Q-Q plot, a scatter plot, and a heat map during EDA, and name one limit of one of these charts.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with univariate checks, one column at a time. For a numeric column I use a box plot. It shows the median, the IQR as the box, and outliers as dots past the whiskers, and side-by-side box plots compare that number across categories. If I need to know whether the column is roughly normal, I use a Q-Q plot. Points on the straight line mean normal, and curving ends mean skew or heavy tails. Then I move to multivariate checks. Two numeric columns go on a scatter plot. Many numeric columns at once go into a correlation heat map, and two categorical columns go into a heat map of counts. One limit is that a box plot hides shape: a distribution with two peaks can look the same as a single-peaked one. Another is that a strong correlation in a heat map does not prove one thing causes the other.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes univariate (one variable) from multivariate (relationships between variables) analysis.
Matches the box plot to the distribution and outliers of a numeric variable, including comparison across categories.
States that a Q-Q plot compares data quantiles to a reference distribution, with a straight line meaning a good fit.
Matches the scatter plot to two numeric variables and the heat map to a correlation matrix or two-category counts.
Names a real limit, such as box plots hiding two-peaked shapes or correlation not implying causation.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine has the learner plot data, and the exam tests picking the right chart for a described dataset, so reasoning through scenario questions builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Real data rarely arrives ready for a model. Some tables are mostly empty (sparse). Some relationships curve instead of following a straight line (non-linear). Some time series drift over time (non-stationary) or repeat on a calendar rhythm (seasonal). Each problem has a usual repair. Text categories can be turned into 0/1 columns (one-hot encoding). Numbers measured on wildly different ranges can be put on a common ruler (scaling). Addresses can be turned into map coordinates (geocoding). Rare cases can be padded out with realistic made-up records (synthetic data). Think of it like prepping ingredients before cooking: the recipe only works if everything is cut to a usable shape.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dataset has an income column in dollars (20,000 to 200,000) and an age column in years (18 to 80). If a model judges how similar two people are by measuring the distance between their numbers, which column do you think will dominate, and why might that be a problem?
lessons.teach:
Four data issues come up again and again. Sparse data means most cells are zero or missing, as in a customer-by-product purchase grid, so each column carries little signal. Non-linearity means the output does not change by a constant amount per unit of input. For example, sales may climb with ad spend and then flatten, so a straight-line model misfits. Fixes include a log transform, polynomial terms (squared or cubed inputs) or a non-linear model. Non-stationarity means a time series' statistics, such as its mean or variance, drift over time. Differencing, which models the change from the previous value rather than the value itself, is a common fix. Seasonality is a repeating calendar pattern, such as weekend or December peaks. You can model it with seasonal terms or remove it by subtracting the value from one cycle earlier.

The remedies each solve a specific problem. One-hot encoding turns a category column into one 0/1 column per category, so the model does not invent a fake order. Scaling puts numeric features on comparable ranges. Standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, and min-max scaling squeezes values into 0 to 1. Geocoding converts addresses into latitude and longitude. Synthetic data is generated records that mimic real ones. It is used to boost rare classes (SMOTE, for example, creates new minority examples between existing ones) or to protect privacy.

Worked example: take columns for income, age and city (Austin, Boston, Denver). Step 1: one-hot encode city, so Austin becomes 1,0,0. Step 2: standardize income and age, so a gap of 50,000 dollars no longer swamps a gap of 30 years. Step 3: a distance-based model now weighs both features fairly. One-hot encoding also adds mostly-zero columns, which creates sparsity. A column with thousands of cities may be better geocoded.

A common mistake is fitting the scaler, or generating synthetic records, on the full dataset before splitting it into training and test sets. Test information then leaks into training, so evaluation scores look better than the model will actually perform in production.

questions.prompt: A city bike-share scheme records daily rentals for three years. An analyst works through it like this. Step 1: a plot shows rentals spike every Saturday and Sunday and dip midweek, repeating every 7 days, so the series has seasonality (a repeating calendar pattern). Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the adjusted series no longer shows the weekly spikes, but its average still creeps upward year after year, so it is also non-stationary (its mean drifts over time). Step 4: the analyst applies differencing, modelling each day's change from the previous day, to remove the drift. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Min-max scale the rental counts so every day falls between 0 and 1
One-hot encode the rental count column into one 0/1 column per value
Subtract from each day's rentals the value from the same weekday 7 days earlier
Use SMOTE to generate extra synthetic weekday records so they match the weekends
questions.why: Seasonality can be removed by subtracting the value from one cycle earlier, and here one cycle is 7 days, which cancels the repeating weekend spike.

questions.prompt: A courier company models delivery cost against parcel weight. Cost barely changes from 1 kg to 15 kg, then climbs much faster for every extra kilogram above 15 kg. A straight-line model badly misfits the heavy parcels. What is the issue, and which remedy fits it?
choices: Sparse data; one-hot encode weight so each kilogram gets its own 0/1 column
Scale mismatch; standardize weight so it has mean 0 and standard deviation 1
Non-stationarity; difference the cost so each value is the change from the previous parcel
Non-linearity; add a polynomial term such as weight squared, or use a non-linear model
questions.why: Cost does not change by a constant amount per kilogram, which is non-linearity, and squared or cubed terms or a non-linear model let the fit bend.

questions.prompt: A clothing retailer stores shirt colour as red = 1, blue = 2, green = 3 and feeds it straight into a regression model. Why is this a problem, and what should be done?
choices: The values are too large compared with other features, so min-max scale them to 0 to 1
The colours should be geocoded into latitude and longitude
The model treats green as 'more' than red, a fake order, so one-hot encode colour into separate 0/1 columns
The column is non-stationary, so difference it before modelling
questions.why: Category codes imply an order that does not exist, and one-hot encoding gives each colour its own 0/1 column so no order is invented.

questions.prompt: A loan team standardizes all 20,000 applicant records (subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation) and then splits them 80/20 into training and test sets. The test score looks excellent, but the deployed model performs noticeably worse on new applicants. What most likely went wrong?
choices: The scaler was fitted on the full dataset before splitting, so test information leaked into training and inflated the test score
The applicant data was sparse, so one-hot encoding should have been applied first
Standardization should never be used on financial data; min-max scaling was required
The 80/20 split was too small; a 50/50 split would have prevented the drop
questions.why: Fitting the scaler before splitting lets the test set's mean and spread shape training, so evaluation looks better than real production performance.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which remedy to apply to a messy dataset: one-hot encoding, scaling, geocoding or synthetic data. Name at least one tradeoff or limit of one of those remedies.
lessons.modelAnswer: I match the remedy to the symptom. If a column holds categories like city names, I one-hot encode it into 0/1 columns, so the model doesn't treat Austin as 'less than' Denver. The tradeoff is that this creates many mostly-zero, sparse columns. With thousands of categories, geocoding into latitude and longitude can be more compact when location is what matters. If numeric features use very different units, like dollars and years, I scale them so distance- or gradient-based models aren't dominated by the big numbers. If a class is rare, synthetic data such as SMOTE can balance it, but fake records can blur real patterns or add noise. Before any of that, I check for non-linearity, trends (non-stationarity) and seasonality, which need transforms or differencing. I always split train and test first, then fit scalers and generate synthetic data on training only, to avoid leakage.
rubricPoints: Links each remedy to the problem it fixes: categories, mismatched ranges, location text, or rare classes.
Explains that one-hot encoding adds sparse columns, and that high-cardinality categories may suit geocoding better.
Notes that scaling matters for distance- or gradient-based models.
Names a limit of synthetic data, such as noise or unrealistic records.
Distinguishes non-stationarity and seasonality, and mentions differencing or seasonal terms.
Warns to fit transforms and generate synthetic data after the train/test split, to avoid leakage.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine works on dataset preparation, and the exam tests choosing the right remedy for a described data symptom, so reasoning through scenario questions builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Building a model is rarely one shot. You loop: decide what limits you must work within, pick a type of model, check what others have already learned, adjust the model's settings, and record every attempt so you can compare and repeat it. Think of perfecting a recipe for a restaurant. The kitchen has a budget and a time limit, which are your constraints. You choose a dish style, read how other chefs made it, tweak oven temperature and cooking time, and keep a notebook of every batch. Without the notebook, you cannot tell which batch was best or make it again.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team tried forty model versions last month but kept no notes. A manager now asks which settings produced the best result and why. What problems do you think the team will run into?
lessons.teach:
The model design iteration process is the repeated cycle of choosing, configuring and testing models until one meets the project's needs. It has five parts.

Design constraints are the limits the model must respect: latency (how fast a prediction must come back), compute and memory budget, interpretability (whether people must understand why it decided something), data volume, privacy rules and deployment target. Set these first because they rule out options early.

Model selection is choosing a model family, such as linear regression, a decision-tree ensemble or a neural network, that fits the problem type and the constraints. Start with a simple baseline, a basic model that every later model must beat.

A literature review is reading published papers, prior internal projects and known benchmarks to learn which approaches already work on similar problems, so you don't reinvent or repeat failures.

Hyperparameter tuning means adjusting settings fixed before training, such as tree depth or learning rate. These differ from parameters, which the model learns from data. Common methods are grid search (try every combination), random search (sample combinations) and Bayesian optimization (use past results to pick promising next tries). Always score candidates on validation data, never the final test set.

Experiment tracking is logging each run's code version, data version, hyperparameters, metrics and artifacts so results are comparable and reproducible.

Worked example: a fraud model must answer in under 50 ms and be explainable to auditors. Step 1: constraints exclude a large deep network. Step 2: the review shows gradient-boosted trees perform well on tabular fraud data. Step 3: a logistic regression baseline scores 0.81 AUC. Step 4: random search over tree depth and learning rate finds depth 6, rate 0.05, giving 0.89 AUC at 20 ms. Step 5: every run is logged, so the winner can be rebuilt exactly.

A common mistake is tuning against the test set. It quietly overfits, so the reported score is inflated. In production the model then performs worse than promised, and without tracking nobody can trace which run or data version caused it.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain wants a model that forecasts next-week demand for each product. It must run on store tablets with only 200 MB of memory, and store managers must be able to understand why it predicts a number. Step 1: The constraints rule out a large neural network. Step 2: A review of an earlier internal project shows that small tree ensembles work well on this kind of sales table. Step 3: A baseline that simply predicts last year's average for the same week gives a mean absolute error (MAE) of 14 units. Step 4 is missing. Step 5: Every run's code version, data version, settings and scores is logged, so the chosen model can be rebuilt exactly. Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Train one tree ensemble, then hand-edit the split values it learned until the MAE drops below 14.
Run Bayesian optimization over tree depth and number of trees, scoring each candidate on held-out validation weeks. Depth 4 with 150 trees reaches an MAE of 10 and fits in memory.
Skip tuning and switch to a large neural network, because a more complex model will beat the baseline anyway.
Run random search over tree depth and number of trees, scoring every candidate on the final test weeks, and keep the one with the lowest test MAE.
questions.why: Step 4 is hyperparameter tuning: it searches settings fixed before training, scores them on validation data rather than the test set, respects the constraints, and beats the baseline.

questions.prompt: A team trains a neural network that predicts when a machine part will fail. Which item is a hyperparameter rather than a parameter?
choices: The bias values the network ends up with after training
The learning rate, which the team chooses before training starts
The connection weights the network adjusts as it learns from the sensor data
The prediction the network outputs for a particular machine
questions.why: A hyperparameter is a setting fixed before training, such as the learning rate. Weights and biases are parameters the model learns from the data.

questions.prompt: A credit union is building a loan-approval model. Regulators require that every rejected applicant be told clearly why they were declined. The data is a modest table of a few thousand past loans. What should the team do first?
choices: Write down interpretability and data volume as design constraints, because they rule out hard-to-explain models before any are built
Tune a large neural network's hyperparameters with grid search to get the highest possible accuracy
Start logging experiments, and decide on interpretability later once a model scores well
Read papers on image recognition to find the newest model architecture
questions.why: Design constraints such as interpretability and data volume are set first because they rule out unsuitable model families early. Here that means models nobody can explain.

questions.prompt: An insurer's team tried 300 hyperparameter combinations. For each one they checked the score on the final test set and kept the best, which reached 0.93 AUC. AUC is a score where 1.0 means the model ranks every case perfectly. In production the model performs at about 0.84. What most likely caused the gap?
choices: Choosing settings by their test-set score quietly overfit the model to that test set, so the 0.93 was inflated
The production servers ran the model too slowly, which lowered its AUC
The model learned too few parameters during training
The team used too few hyperparameter combinations, so the search was not thorough enough
questions.why: Tuning against the test set leaks it into the model choice. The reported score is inflated, and real-world performance comes in lower than promised.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would iterate on a model design from constraints through experiment tracking, and name one tradeoff you would face, such as accuracy versus latency or tuning effort versus cost.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by writing down the constraints, like latency, budget, interpretability and privacy, because they eliminate model types before I waste time on them. Then I do a quick literature review of papers, past projects and benchmarks to see what works on similar data. I build a simple baseline and select candidate model families that fit the constraints. Next I tune hyperparameters, the settings chosen before training, using random or Bayesian search scored on validation data, keeping the test set untouched until the end. Every run gets logged with its code version, data version, settings and metrics, so we can compare runs fairly and reproduce the winner. The main tradeoff is accuracy versus constraints. A bigger model might score higher but break our latency or explainability limits. Exhaustive tuning also costs compute and time, so I stop when gains become small.
rubricPoints: Constraints are defined first and used to narrow model choices.
A literature review and a simple baseline guide model selection.
Hyperparameters are distinguished from learned parameters and tuned on validation data, not the test set.
Experiment tracking records code, data, hyperparameters and metrics for comparison and reproducibility.
At least one tradeoff is named, such as accuracy versus latency or tuning cost.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine runs model tuning, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario that weighs constraints, tuning method and tracking adds the most.

lessons.plain: Once you have trained several candidate models, you must pick one and defend that pick with evidence, not gut feeling. That means scoring each model fairly on data it has never seen, looking at pictures of its mistakes to spot hidden problems, comparing it to a simple 'dumb' reference so you know it adds value, and checking it against the real requirements, such as speed or how many cases it must catch. It is like choosing a new hire: you check test results, watch how they handle tricky cases, compare them to the current baseline, and confirm they meet the job description.
lessons.guessPrompt: A disease-screening model scores 97% accuracy, but 97% of the patients in the data are healthy. Do you think 97% accuracy proves the model is useful? What simple comparison would you make before believing it?
lessons.teach:
A final model recommendation is a justified choice of one model, backed by four kinds of evidence.

Performance evaluation means scoring each candidate on a test set, data held back and never used for training or tuning, with a metric that fits the problem: accuracy (share of predictions correct), precision (of items flagged positive, the share truly positive), recall (of truly positive items, the share caught), or RMSE, root mean squared error, the typical size of a numeric prediction's miss.

Diagnostic plots show why a score looks the way it does. A residual plot charts each error (actual minus predicted) against the prediction; random scatter is healthy, while a curve or funnel shape means the model misses a pattern or is less reliable at some values. A confusion matrix is a table counting correct and incorrect predictions per class. A learning curve plots training and validation scores as data grows; a large gap signals overfitting, meaning the model memorized training data instead of learning general patterns.

Benchmarking compares candidates against a baseline, a deliberately simple reference such as always predicting the most common class, proving the model adds real value. Requirements validation checks the winner against stated needs: minimum recall, prediction time, model size, explainability.

Worked example: a fraud model must catch at least 80% of fraud and respond within 50 ms; fraud is 2% of transactions. Step 1: the baseline 'never fraud' scores 98% accuracy, so accuracy is useless here; use recall and precision. Step 2: Model A, a complex ensemble, has recall 0.86 and takes 120 ms. Model B, logistic regression, has recall 0.82 and takes 8 ms. Step 3: B's confusion matrix shows acceptable false alarms, and its learning curve shows a small gap. Step 4: A fails the latency requirement; B passes both. Recommend B, citing each piece of evidence.

Common mistake: crowning the model with the best headline number, often accuracy on imbalanced data or a score from data also used for tuning, which inflates it. In production that model disappoints: fraud slips through or requests time out, and stakeholders stop trusting the team.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility needs a model that predicts tomorrow's total water demand in megaliters (ML). The stated requirements are a test-set RMSE (root mean squared error, the typical size of a prediction's miss) of no more than 40 ML, and a model simple enough that its reasoning can be explained to the utility's regulator. Step 1: on a held-back test set, Model P, a gradient-boosted ensemble, scores an RMSE of 31 ML. Model Q, a linear regression, scores 37 ML. Step 2: a baseline that simply predicts yesterday's demand scores 74 ML, so both candidates add real value. Step 3: Q's residual plot shows random scatter with no curve or funnel, and its learning curve shows only a small gap between training and validation scores. Step 4: ______. Step 5: recommend Model Q, citing the test score, the baseline comparison, the diagnostic plots and the requirements check. What belongs in Step 4?
choices: Recommend Model P instead, because its 31 ML RMSE is the best score and so it should win.
Check both models against the stated needs: P meets the RMSE limit but cannot be explained to the regulator, while Q meets both.
Re-score both models with accuracy, since accuracy is the most widely understood metric for stakeholders.
Retune both models on the test set until each one's RMSE falls well below 40 ML.
questions.why: Requirements validation checks candidates against every stated need, and only Q passes both the RMSE limit and the explainability requirement, which is what justifies recommending it over the lower-scoring P.

questions.prompt: A tool manufacturer builds a model to flag defective drills on its production line. About 3% of drills are defective. The data science team reports that the model scored 97% accuracy on a held-back test set and proposes deploying it. What is the most important problem with this evidence?
choices: The team should have plotted residuals instead, because tables of scores cannot be benchmarked.
A 97% score is too high to be realistic, so the test set must have been used during training.
A baseline that always predicts 'not defective' would also score about 97% accuracy, so the result shows no added value; recall and precision are needed.
Accuracy only works for numeric predictions, so the team should have reported RMSE.
questions.why: When one class dominates, a trivial baseline already reaches high accuracy, so accuracy cannot show that the model actually catches defects.

questions.prompt: An apartment-rental site builds a model that predicts monthly rent. On its residual plot, which charts each error (actual minus predicted) against the predicted rent, the points sit tightly around zero for low predicted rents but spread out wider and wider as predicted rent rises, forming a funnel. What does this tell the team?
choices: The baseline must be replaced, because a funnel shape means the baseline was too simple.
The model has memorized its training data, which is shown by the funnel being wide.
The model is healthy, because the residuals are centred on zero overall.
The model's predictions are less reliable for higher-priced apartments than for cheaper ones.
questions.why: A funnel-shaped residual plot means the size of the errors changes with the prediction, so the model is less reliable at the values where the spread is widest.

questions.prompt: A logistics team compares three delivery-time models. They adjust each model's settings repeatedly until it does best on one dataset, then report each model's RMSE on that same dataset and recommend the lowest one. Why is this recommendation weak?
choices: RMSE cannot compare models of different types, so precision should have been used.
The team compared three models instead of exactly two, which makes benchmarking invalid.
Tuning should only be done after a model is deployed, never before it is evaluated.
The scores are inflated because the data used for tuning was also used for the final evaluation, so the winner will likely disappoint in production.
questions.why: A fair performance score must come from a test set never used for training or tuning; scoring on the tuning data makes every model look better than it will be on new data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would justify recommending one model over another after an experiment, and name one tradeoff or limit that could make the 'best-scoring' model the wrong choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd start by scoring every candidate on a held-out test set that was never used for training or tuning, using a metric that matches the goal, like recall when missing positives is costly, or RMSE for numeric predictions. Then I'd look at diagnostic plots: residual plots for patterns or funnels, a confusion matrix to see which errors happen, and learning curves to spot overfitting. Next I'd benchmark against a simple baseline, such as always predicting the majority class, so we know the model actually adds value. Finally I'd validate against requirements like latency, size, and explainability. The tradeoff is that the highest-scoring model can fail a hard requirement: a complex model might gain a few points of recall but be too slow to serve in time, so a simpler model that meets every requirement is the better recommendation.
rubricPoints: Evaluates candidates on a held-out test set not used for training or tuning.
Chooses a metric that fits the problem, noting accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.
Uses diagnostic plots such as residual plots, confusion matrices, or learning curves to explain errors.
Compares against a simple baseline to show real added value.
Checks the winner against stated requirements like latency, recall threshold, or explainability.
Names a tradeoff, such as a higher score coming with failed requirements.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine evaluates models, and the skill is best built by reasoning through exam-style scenarios that weigh metrics, plots, baselines, and requirements to pick a model.

lessons.plain: Communicating results means turning what an analysis found into something a specific person can understand and act on. Different listeners need different things. A busy executive wants the decision and its impact in one glance. A domain expert, such as a doctor or a logistics manager, wants to see how the finding fits their field. A fellow data scientist wants the methods and numbers so they can check the work. A good chart is like a map: it should be honest about distances and readable by everyone who uses it, including people who cannot tell red from green.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bar chart compares two models' accuracy, 96% and 98%, but the vertical axis starts at 95% instead of 0%. What impression might a busy executive get from that chart, and would that impression be accurate?
lessons.teach:
Translating results means fitting the format to the audience. An executive audience is senior decision-makers. Give them a short summary that leads with the recommendation, the business impact (money, risk, time), and one or two simple charts such as a bar or line chart. A domain audience is subject-matter experts outside data science. Give them results in their own terms and units, with the caveats that matter in their field. A peer audience is other analysts. Give them a technical report covering methods, metrics, assumptions, diagnostic plots, and enough detail to reproduce the work.

Deceptive charting is any design choice that makes the data look different from what it is, even by accident. Common forms are: a truncated axis, meaning a bar chart's value axis does not start at zero; dual axes, meaning two series sharing one chart with independent scales, which can make them look correlated; 3D effects or pie slices that distort size; and cherry-picked time ranges.

Accessibility means everyone can read the chart. Use colorblind-safe palettes, never rely on color alone (add labels, patterns, or shapes), keep high contrast and readable fonts, and provide alt text, a short written description for screen-reader users.

Worked example: churn, meaning the share of customers who leave, fell from 4.1% to 3.8% after a new model. Step 1: a bar chart with its axis starting at 3.7% makes the second bar look less than half as tall. Step 2: the real relative drop is 0.3 divided by 4.1, about 7%. Step 3: redraw with the axis at zero, label both values, and state "about 7% fewer customers leaving, roughly X dollars per year" for executives.

A common mistake is sending one deck to every audience: executives drown in metrics and peers lack the detail to verify. In a running business, a misleading or unreadable chart can drive a funding or launch decision on an exaggerated effect and erode trust in every later report.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital's 30-day readmission rate (the share of discharged patients who return within a month) fell from 12.0% to 11.4% after a new discharge-planning model. Step 1: A draft bar chart starts its value axis at 11%, so the second bar looks roughly half as tall as the first. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: Redraw the chart with the axis starting at zero, label both bars 12.0% and 11.4%, and give executives the true relative improvement along with its estimated cost savings. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Report the drop as about 95%, because 11.4 divided by 12.0 is 0.95
Report the drop as about 0.6%, because the rate moved from 12.0 to 11.4
Report the drop as about 50%, because that matches how the bars look
Work out the real relative drop: 0.6 divided by 12.0, which is about 5%
questions.why: The relative drop is the change (0.6 points) divided by the starting value (12.0), which is about 5%. The truncated axis made it look like about 50%.

questions.prompt: An analyst has built a crop-yield model for a team of agronomists. Agronomists are farm-science experts who are not data scientists. Which presentation best fits this domain audience?
choices: Yield results in bushels per acre, with the caveats that matter in farming, such as weather and soil conditions
The same slide deck prepared for the executives, so every group sees identical material
A full technical report covering hyperparameters, residual plots, and code so the work can be reproduced
A one-slide summary that leads with a funding recommendation and the dollar impact, with no other detail
questions.why: A domain audience needs results in its own terms and units, plus the field-specific caveats. The other options suit executives or peers, or repeat the one-deck-for-everyone mistake.

questions.prompt: A marketing team shows monthly ad spend and monthly app sign-ups on one chart. Each series has its own independently scaled vertical axis. Both lines appear to rise in lockstep, and the team concludes that ad spend drives sign-ups. What is the main charting problem?
choices: The chart should be a pie chart, so each month's share is visible
The bar chart's value axis is truncated because it does not start at zero
Dual axes with independent scales can make two series look correlated even when they are not
The chart uses a cherry-picked palette that is not colorblind-safe
questions.why: With dual axes, each scale can be stretched independently until the two lines appear to move together. That is a form of deceptive charting.

questions.prompt: A logistics dashboard shows on-time deliveries as a green line and late deliveries as a red line. There are no labels or markers, and the chart has no written description. Which fix best addresses accessibility?
choices: Switch to a 3D chart so the two series are easier to tell apart
Use a colorblind-safe palette, add direct labels or distinct marker shapes, and provide alt text
Make the red line brighter so late deliveries stand out more
Remove the late-delivery line so only one color remains
questions.why: Accessibility means not relying on color alone. That calls for a colorblind-safe palette, labels or shapes on each line, and alt text, a short written description that screen-reader users can hear.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would present the same model result to an executive, a domain expert, and a fellow data scientist, and name one tradeoff you accept when simplifying for the executive.
lessons.modelAnswer: I tailor the format to who is deciding what. For the executive, I lead with the recommendation and business impact in plain terms, with one honest chart: a bar chart starting at zero, values labeled, no 3D or dual axes. For the domain expert, I express results in their units and highlight caveats that matter in their field, like which customer segments the model handles poorly. For a peer, I write a technical report with metrics, assumptions, diagnostic plots, and enough detail to reproduce it. In every version I use colorblind-safe colors, don't rely on color alone, and add alt text. The tradeoff with executives is that simplifying drops uncertainty and edge cases, so I state the key limitation in one sentence and point to the full report instead of hiding it.
rubricPoints: Executives get the recommendation and business impact first, with few simple charts.
Domain experts get results in their own terms and units with field-relevant caveats.
Peers get methods, metrics, assumptions, and reproducible detail.
Avoids deceptive charts such as truncated axes, dual axes, 3D distortion, or cherry-picked ranges.
Ensures accessibility with colorblind-safe palettes, non-color cues, contrast, and alt text.
Names a tradeoff, such as simplification hiding uncertainty, and how to mitigate it.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through audience and chart scenarios, so reasoning through situations like a truncated-axis chart or an executive briefing builds the judgment best.

lessons.plain: Documentation is the written record that lets someone other than the original author understand, trust, and safely change a dataset or model. Three kinds matter most. A data dictionary explains each column: what it means, its type, its units, and its allowed values. Metadata is data about the data, such as where it came from, who owns it, and when it was refreshed. Change descriptions record what changed, why, and when. Think of a shared kitchen: labels on jars, a note on when the groceries were bought, and a log saying someone swapped sugar for salt.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's model uses a column called "dist". The original author has left. Without any written notes, what could go wrong if you assume the values are in miles?
lessons.teach:
Documentation for data and models is any written record that explains what the data and code mean, where they came from, and how they have changed. Three forms carry most of the weight.

A data dictionary is a table that describes every field (column) in a dataset: its name, its data type (number, text, date), its units, its allowed values or range, what a missing value means, and a plain-language definition. Metadata is data about the data as a whole: its source system, owner, collection date, refresh schedule, row count, version number, and lineage (the chain of steps that produced it). A change description is a short record attached to each update of data, code, or a model, stating what changed, why, who changed it, when, and what it might affect. Changelogs, version-control commit messages, and model version notes are all change descriptions.

These work because a model's behavior depends on assumptions that are invisible in the numbers themselves. Writing the assumptions down makes results reproducible, makes handoffs possible, and gives auditors and debuggers a trail to follow.

Worked example. A delivery-time model uses the field "dist". Step 1: the data dictionary says "dist: trip distance, decimal, miles, range 0 to 500". Step 2: next quarter the upstream team switches to kilometers and writes a change description: "v2.0, dist now in km, effective March 1, affects downstream models". Step 3: the metadata shows the training set is v1.4 but new scoring data is v2.0. Step 4: the analyst spots the mismatch, adds a conversion, updates the dictionary, and records the model change. Without these records, the model would quietly treat 100 km as 100 miles and predictions would drift.

A common mistake is documenting once at launch and never updating it. Stale documentation is worse than none because people trust it. In a running system, missing or outdated documentation leads to silent errors, results nobody can reproduce, slow incident response, and failed compliance reviews.

questions.prompt: A subscription streaming company has a churn model that uses the field "plan_status". Step 1: the data dictionary says "plan_status: integer code, allowed values 1 = active, 2 = cancelled". Step 2: the billing team adds a new option and writes a change description: "v5.2, plan_status now includes 3 = paused, effective June 10, affects churn reporting and models". Step 3: ______. Step 4: the analyst sees the model was trained only on codes 1 and 2, decides how code 3 should be handled, updates the data dictionary to list code 3, and records a model change note. Which action best fills Step 3?
choices: The analyst checks the metadata and finds the training set is version 5.1 while the new scoring data is version 5.2
The analyst deletes every row with code 3 from the scoring data so the model sees only familiar values
The analyst trusts the data dictionary, which still lists only codes 1 and 2, and treats any 3 as a data entry error
The analyst retrains the model on the newest data right away without reading the change description
questions.why: Comparing the version numbers in the metadata is what reveals that the model was trained on older data than the data it is now scoring, which is the mismatch Step 4 acts on.

questions.prompt: A hospital analytics team writes this note about its patient-visits table: "Source: electronic health record system. Owner: clinical data team. Refreshed nightly at 2 a.m. About 1.8 million rows. Version 3.0. Built by joining the admissions and billing extracts." Which form of documentation is this?
choices: A data dictionary, because it describes the type, units, and allowed values of each column
A change description, because it records what was altered in the latest update and why
Code comments, because it explains how individual lines of a script work
Metadata, because it describes the dataset as a whole: source, owner, refresh schedule, size, version, and lineage
questions.why: Information about the dataset as a whole, such as its source, owner, refresh schedule, row count, version, and lineage, is metadata rather than a per-field description or a record of a single change.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a regional bank changes the fraud model's feature script so that transaction amounts are rounded to whole dollars. Which commit message is the most useful change description?
choices: "Fixed stuff in the features file"
"Round txn_amount to whole dollars to match new ledger format; by R. Patel, May 3; may shift fraud scores near thresholds"
"Rounding added. Thanks to the team for the help!"
"Updated fraud model, see code for details"
