questions.why: A good change description states what changed, why, who made the change, when, and what it might affect, and only that message covers all five.

questions.prompt: A logistics company wrote a detailed data dictionary when it launched its warehouse dataset two years ago and has not touched it since. Upstream teams have renamed and redefined several fields in that time. What is the main risk?
choices: The dataset's row count will drop, because old dictionary entries remove fields that no longer match
None, because a dictionary written carefully at launch stays accurate as long as the field names exist
Analysts trust the outdated definitions, so they can make silent errors that are harder to catch than if no dictionary existed
The model will stop running immediately, because software checks the dictionary before every prediction
questions.why: Stale documentation is worse than none because people trust it, which leads to silent errors, results nobody can reproduce, and slower incident response.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a data dictionary, metadata, and a change description, and name one cost or limit of keeping documentation.
lessons.modelAnswer: A data dictionary works at the column level. It tells you what each field means, its type, units, allowed values, and how missing values are handled. Metadata works at the dataset or model level. It records the source, owner, refresh date, version, and lineage, so you know whether this is the data you think it is. A change description records each update: what changed, why, who made it, when, and what it affects. Together they let someone else reproduce our results, catch mismatches like a unit change, and audit decisions. The tradeoff is upkeep. Documentation takes time to maintain, and if we let it go stale it becomes actively harmful, because people trust it and act on wrong information. So updating the docs has to be part of every change, not a separate chore we save for later.
rubricPoints: Defines a data dictionary as per-field meaning, type, units, and allowed values.
Defines metadata as data about the dataset, such as source, owner, version, and lineage.
Defines change descriptions as records of what changed, why, when, and by whom.
Links documentation to reproducibility, handoff, debugging, or auditing.
Names a limit, such as maintenance cost or the danger of stale documentation.

suggested.rationale: Exam items on this objective usually present a scenario, such as a unit change or a handoff, and ask which documentation artifact would have prevented the problem, so reasoning through situations builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Machine learning means letting a computer learn a pattern from examples instead of writing the rules by hand. A few core ideas decide whether that pattern is any good. Picture a student preparing for an exam. They need a marking scheme that says how wrong each answer is (a loss function). They should understand the material rather than memorize past papers (avoiding overfitting). They should take practice tests they have never seen (cross-validation) and compare notes with a study group (ensembles). They must also notice when the syllabus changes (drift). The rest of this lesson builds on that picture.
lessons.guessPrompt: A fraud model is trained on data where 1 in 100 transactions is fraud. It labels every transaction 'not fraud' and scores 99% accuracy. Is it a good model, and what would you change?
lessons.teach:
A loss function scores how wrong a prediction is, and training adjusts the model to shrink the total loss. Mean squared error, the average squared gap between prediction and truth, suits numeric targets. Cross-entropy, also called log loss, punishes confident wrong probabilities and suits classification.

Bias is error from a model too simple to capture the pattern, which is called underfitting. Variance is error from a model so flexible it memorizes noise in its training data, which is called overfitting. Lowering one usually raises the other, so you aim for the lowest error on new data.

Regularization adds a penalty for large model weights to the loss. A weight is a number the model learns that sets how strongly a feature affects the prediction. The L1 penalty can push weights to exactly zero. The L2 penalty shrinks all of them smoothly.

Cross-validation estimates performance on unseen data. In k-fold cross-validation you split the data into k parts. You train on k-1 parts, score on the held-out part, rotate through all k parts, and average the scores.

An ensemble combines several models. Bagging averages models trained on resampled data to cut variance. Boosting trains models in sequence, each one correcting earlier errors, to cut bias.

Class imbalance means one outcome is rare. Random oversampling duplicates rows of the rare class. SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) creates new rare rows by blending a rare example with a nearby rare neighbor.

Worked example: take 10,000 transactions, 100 of them fraud. Always predicting 'not fraud' gives 99% accuracy but catches zero fraud. So you judge the model by recall (the share of real fraud it catches) and precision (the share of its fraud flags that are correct). Split the data into 5 folds. In each round, apply SMOTE only to the 4 training folds, train, and score on the untouched fifth fold, which keeps its real 1% fraud rate. Then average the five scores.

The common mistake is oversampling before splitting. Copies of test rows leak into training, and the score looks better than reality.

Model drift is decay after deployment. Data drift means the inputs shift. Concept drift means the link between inputs and outcome changes, for example when fraudsters adopt new tactics. A deployed model can quietly lose accuracy, so you monitor it and retrain on fresh data.

questions.prompt: A water utility builds a deep decision tree to predict daily pipe-burst counts from 40 sensor features. The work so far: (1) Because the target is a number, the team scores it with mean squared error. (2) Using 5-fold cross-validation, the average training error is 3 and the average error on the held-out folds is 45. (3) A training error far below the held-out error means the tree has memorized noise in its training data. That is high variance, or overfitting. (4) MISSING STEP: choose a remedy aimed at that diagnosis. (5) Rerun the same 5-fold cross-validation and keep the change only if the held-out error drops. Which choice best completes step 4?
choices: Switch to boosting, so that each new model in the sequence corrects the errors of the earlier ones.
Make the model more flexible by adding more features and allowing a deeper tree, so it captures more of the pattern.
Add an L2 penalty on large weights to the loss, or average many models trained on resampled data (bagging).
Swap mean squared error for cross-entropy, so that confident wrong predictions are punished more heavily.
questions.why: Regularization and bagging both rein in an overly flexible model and so reduce variance, while boosting and extra flexibility target bias, and cross-entropy is a loss for classification rather than numeric targets.

questions.prompt: A clinic has 3,000 patient records, and 90 of them have a rare condition. An analyst randomly oversamples the rare class across the whole dataset first, then runs 5-fold cross-validation and reports recall of 0.95. After deployment, recall on new patients is only about 0.55. What most likely explains the gap?
choices: The L1 penalty pushed the important weights to zero during training.
The model underfit because oversampling made it too simple to capture the pattern.
Duplicated rare rows ended up in both the training and test folds, so the cross-validation score was inflated by leakage.
Recall is the wrong measure here, and accuracy would have shown the true performance.
questions.why: Oversampling before splitting lets copies of test rows leak into training, so the cross-validated score looks better than real-world performance.

questions.prompt: A retailer's model predicts which customers will respond to a promotion. It uses 300 features, and the team suspects most of them are useless. They want a regularization penalty that can remove useless features entirely by setting their weights to exactly zero. Which should they choose?
choices: The L2 penalty, because it shrinks every weight smoothly toward zero.
Bagging, because averaging resampled models cuts variance.
SMOTE, because it blends nearby examples to balance the classes.
The L1 penalty, because it can push weights to exactly zero.
questions.why: The L1 penalty can drive weights to exactly zero, which effectively drops those features, whereas L2 only shrinks weights without zeroing them.

questions.prompt: A lender's loan-default model was accurate at launch. A year later, the applicants' incomes, debts and credit histories look much the same as before. However, after a change in the economy, applicants with those same profiles now default at a very different rate, and the model's accuracy has quietly fallen. What is this, and what is the usual response?
choices: Data drift: the inputs have shifted, so apply SMOTE to the original training data.
Overfitting: the model memorized noise, so increase k in k-fold cross-validation.
Class imbalance: defaults are rare, so judge the model by accuracy instead of recall.
Concept drift: the link between the inputs and the outcome has changed, so monitor the model and retrain it on fresh data.
questions.why: The inputs are unchanged but their relationship to defaulting has changed, which is concept drift, and the remedy is monitoring the model and retraining it on fresh data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a model with near-perfect training accuracy might still be a bad model, using the bias-variance tradeoff, cross-validation, and one limit of fixing class imbalance with SMOTE.
lessons.modelAnswer: High training accuracy can just mean the model memorized its data. That is high variance, or overfitting. Its error on new data will be much worse. The opposite failure is high bias, where the model is too simple and misses the real pattern. To find the balance, we use k-fold cross-validation: train on most of the data, score on a held-out fold, rotate, and average. That gives an honest estimate on unseen data. Regularization helps by penalizing large weights, which pulls the model toward simplicity. If the target is rare, like fraud, accuracy itself misleads, so we look at recall and precision. SMOTE creates synthetic rare examples, but it has limits. It must run only on training folds, or synthetic copies leak test information. It can also invent unrealistic points near the class boundary. Even a good model drifts after deployment, so we monitor and retrain.
rubricPoints: Defines overfitting as high variance and underfitting as high bias, and says reducing one tends to raise the other.
Explains that cross-validation scores the model on held-out data it did not train on.
Notes that accuracy misleads under class imbalance and names a better metric such as recall or precision.
States that SMOTE or oversampling must be applied only to training data to avoid leakage.
Mentions regularization or ensembles as a way to control the tradeoff.
Recognizes that deployed models drift and need monitoring and retraining.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine trains models, and the exam tests these ideas through scenarios where you must pick the right fix, such as a metric, resampling, regularization or retraining, so reasoning through exam-style cases adds the most.

lessons.plain: These are the classic statistics-based ways to make predictions from labelled examples. Linear regression predicts a number, such as a price. Logistic regression predicts the chance of a yes or no, such as spam or not spam. Ridge, LASSO and elastic net are versions of these that are kept from overreacting to noise. Discriminant analysis sorts items into groups by how each group's data is spread. Naive Bayes classifies quickly by combining simple probabilities. Association rules find items that tend to show up together, like bread and butter in shopping baskets. Think of a toolbox: each tool fits one kind of job.
lessons.guessPrompt: Out of 1,000 shopping baskets, 300 contain butter. Among the 200 baskets that contain bread, 150 also contain butter. Does buying bread seem to make butter more likely than usual? Roughly how much more?
lessons.teach:
Supervised learning means training on examples that already carry the correct answer, called a label. Each input column is a feature.

Linear regression predicts a number. It fits a weighted sum of the features and picks the weights, called coefficients, that make the squared prediction errors as small as possible. Logistic regression predicts the probability of a yes/no class. It passes that weighted sum through an S-shaped curve that keeps the result between 0 and 1.

With many features, or with correlated ones, coefficients can swing wildly and the model can overfit, meaning it memorises noise. Regularization adds a penalty for large coefficients. Ridge (an L2 penalty, based on squared coefficients) shrinks every coefficient toward zero but keeps all the features. LASSO (an L1 penalty, based on the size of each coefficient) can push some coefficients exactly to zero, so it also selects features. Elastic net blends the two penalties and suits groups of correlated features.

Discriminant analysis treats each class as a bell-shaped (normal) cloud of points. LDA (linear discriminant analysis) assumes every class has the same spread, so it draws straight boundaries between classes. QDA (quadratic discriminant analysis) gives each class its own spread, so its boundaries can curve.

Naive Bayes applies Bayes' theorem, a rule for updating a probability when you see evidence. It assumes features are independent of each other once you know the class. That assumption is "naive", but the method is fast and works well on text.

Association rules find if-then patterns in transaction data, such as {bread} → {butter}. Three scores rate a rule. Support is how often the items appear together. Confidence is how often the then-part appears when the if-part does. Lift is confidence divided by how common the then-part is overall. These rules need no label, but exams group them here.

Worked example with 1,000 baskets. Step 1: 150 baskets contain both bread and butter, so support = 0.15. Step 2: 200 contain bread, so confidence = 150/200 = 0.75. Step 3: 300 contain butter, so butter's base rate = 0.30. Step 4: lift = 0.75/0.30 = 2.5. A lift of 1 would mean no association.

A common mistake is using linear regression for a yes/no outcome. It can output "probabilities" below 0 or above 1. In a production system, choosing LASSO yields a leaner model that is cheaper to serve. However, it may drop one of two useful correlated features.

questions.prompt: A hardware retailer reviews 2,000 online orders to rate the rule {paint} → {brushes}. Step 1: 120 orders contain both paint and brushes, so support = 120/2,000 = 0.06. Step 2: 400 orders contain paint, so confidence = 120/400 = 0.30. Step 3: 500 orders contain brushes, so the base rate of brushes = 500/2,000 = 0.25. Step 4 is missing: what is the lift of this rule, and what does it suggest?
choices: Lift = 0.06 / 0.25 = 0.24, meaning paint buyers avoid brushes
Lift = 0.25 / 0.30 = 0.83, meaning no real association
Lift = 0.30 / 0.25 = 1.2, a mild positive association
Lift = 0.30 / 0.06 = 5.0, a very strong association
questions.why: Lift is confidence divided by the then-part's base rate, so 0.30 / 0.25 = 1.2, which is just above 1 and signals a mild positive association.

questions.prompt: A factory team predicts machine energy use (a number) from 300 sensor readings, many of which are probably irrelevant. They want a regression model that automatically drops useless sensors so the deployed model stays small and cheap to run. Which technique fits best?
choices: Logistic regression, because it keeps outputs between 0 and 1
Ridge regression, because its L2 penalty removes the least useful features
LASSO regression, because its L1 penalty can set some coefficients exactly to zero
Quadratic discriminant analysis, because it allows curved boundaries
questions.why: LASSO's L1 penalty can push coefficients exactly to zero, which removes those features, while ridge only shrinks coefficients and keeps every feature.

questions.prompt: An analyst at a gym chain uses plain linear regression to predict whether a member will cancel (1) or stay (0). For some members the model outputs 1.3 and for others -0.2. What is the underlying problem?
choices: Linear regression always overfits when the label has only two values
Linear regression predicts an unbounded number; a yes/no outcome calls for logistic regression
The model needs a ridge penalty to bring the outputs back into range
The features must be independent, so naive Bayes assumptions are violated
questions.why: Linear regression outputs any number, so its "probabilities" can fall below 0 or above 1, whereas logistic regression passes the weighted sum through an S-shaped curve that keeps results between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: A bank classifies loan applicants into three risk groups. Plotting the data shows each group forms a roughly bell-shaped cloud, but one group is tightly packed while another is widely spread out. Which discriminant method suits this data better, and why?
choices: LDA, because it gives each class its own spread and draws straight boundaries
LDA, because it assumes all classes share the same spread, matching this data
Naive Bayes, because discriminant analysis cannot handle more than two classes
QDA, because it lets each class have its own spread, so boundaries can curve
questions.why: QDA allows each class its own spread, which matches groups with clearly different spreads, while LDA assumes every class shares the same spread.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose among ridge, LASSO, elastic net, logistic regression, LDA, naive Bayes and association rules for a new problem. Include one limitation or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I ask what we are predicting. If it is a number, I start with linear regression. If it is a yes/no class, I use logistic regression, because it returns a proper probability between 0 and 1. If there are many or correlated features, I add regularization. Ridge shrinks every coefficient but keeps all features. LASSO can zero some out, which gives a smaller, easier-to-explain model, though it may drop one of two correlated features at random. Elastic net blends both penalties and handles correlated groups. For classes that look like bell-shaped clouds, LDA draws straight boundaries and QDA allows curved ones. For text, naive Bayes is fast, but its assumption that features are independent is rarely true. If there is no label and we want items that co-occur, I use association rules scored by support, confidence and lift. High lift shows the items go together, not that one causes the other.
rubricPoints: Matches the output type: linear regression for a number, logistic regression for a class probability.
Distinguishes ridge (shrinks all coefficients), LASSO (zeroes some out, selecting features) and elastic net (blends both).
Describes discriminant analysis as modelling classes as normal distributions, with LDA giving linear boundaries and QDA curved ones.
States that naive Bayes assumes features are independent given the class.
Defines association rules and at least one of support, confidence or lift.
Names a real limitation or tradeoff, such as LASSO dropping a correlated feature or lift not implying causation.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right statistical technique for a described scenario, and no current mission or planned engine does that, so reasoning through exam-style situations helps most.

lessons.plain: A decision tree makes a prediction the way a game of twenty questions does: it asks a series of yes-or-no questions about something, such as whether income is above 40,000 or whether the customer is new, until it reaches an answer. One tree is easy to follow but often fragile. Two tricks make trees stronger. A random forest builds many trees on slightly different copies of the data and lets them vote, like asking a crowd instead of one person. Boosting builds trees one after another, with each new tree trying to fix the mistakes the earlier ones made.
lessons.guessPrompt: One person guessing the number of beans in a jar is often far off. Would averaging 100 people's guesses usually get closer to the truth? Why would it matter that those people do not all copy one another's guess?
lessons.teach:
A decision tree predicts by asking a chain of yes/no questions about the features, which are the input columns. Each question is a split at a node. The end points are leaves, and each leaf holds the prediction: a class for classification, or an average value for regression. During training, the tree chooses at each node the split that best separates the target. It measures this with impurity, a score of how mixed the labels in a group are; Gini impurity and entropy are the common ones. Trees are readable, but deep ones overfit, meaning they memorize noise and do worse on new data. They also have high variance: a small change in the data can produce a very different tree.

Bootstrap aggregation, also called bagging, reduces that variance. A bootstrap sample is a random draw of rows, the same size as the training set, taken with replacement, so some rows repeat and others are left out. You train one tree per sample and then aggregate the trees: a majority vote for classes, an average for numbers. A random forest is bagged trees with one addition: each split may only consider a random subset of features. This makes the trees more different from one another, so their errors cancel out better when combined.

Boosting builds trees in sequence instead of side by side. Each new shallow tree is fitted to the residuals, which are the errors the ensemble still makes. Its output is then added after being scaled by a learning rate, a small multiplier that slows the correction. XGBoost (extreme gradient boosting) is a fast, widely used boosting library that also penalizes tree complexity.

Worked example: the true house price is 300. Tree one predicts 250, so the residual is 50. Tree two learns that residual and predicts 40. With a learning rate of 0.5, the ensemble adds 20, giving 270. The new residual is 30, and tree three targets that.

A common mistake is treating random forest and boosting as the same thing. Bagging mainly cuts variance, and adding more trees rarely causes overfitting. Boosting mainly cuts bias and overfits if it runs too many rounds without a holdout check. An overfit boosted model can look excellent in testing and then degrade on live data.

questions.prompt: A courier company uses gradient boosting to predict delivery time in minutes. For one parcel, the true delivery time is 60 minutes. Step 1: tree one predicts 45, so the residual (the error still left) is 60 - 45 = 15. Step 2: tree two is fitted to that residual and predicts 12. Step 3: the learning rate (the small multiplier that slows each correction) is 0.25. [Missing step: what is the ensemble's prediction after tree two is added?] Step 4: the new residual is then calculated, and tree three is fitted to it.
choices: 57 minutes, because tree two's output of 12 is added to 45 in full
48 minutes, because 12 x 0.25 = 3 is added to 45
3 minutes, because the ensemble now uses only tree two's scaled output
60 minutes, because tree two fully corrects the remaining error
questions.why: In boosting, the new tree's output is scaled by the learning rate (12 x 0.25 = 3) and then added to the existing prediction (45 + 3 = 48).

questions.prompt: A retailer has a training set of 1,000 customer rows and uses bootstrap aggregation (bagging) to build an ensemble of decision trees. Which description matches one bootstrap sample used to train one of those trees?
choices: All 1,000 rows, but each split may look at only a random subset of the columns
1,000 rows drawn at random with replacement, so some rows repeat and some are left out
500 rows chosen at random, with the other 500 kept aside for testing
The same 1,000 rows in a shuffled order, with each row appearing exactly once
questions.why: A bootstrap sample is the same size as the training set and is drawn with replacement, which is why some rows repeat and others are missed.

questions.prompt: A bank's fraud team trains 200 decision trees, each on its own bootstrap sample, and combines them by majority vote. They notice almost every tree makes its first split on transaction amount, so the trees make similar errors. Which change turns this bagged ensemble into a random forest?
choices: Allow each split to consider only a random subset of the features
Switch the impurity measure from Gini impurity to entropy
Build the trees one after another, each fitted to the previous trees' residuals
Increase the number of trees from 200 to 2,000 without changing anything else
questions.why: A random forest is bagging plus a random subset of features at each split, which makes the trees more different so their errors cancel out better.

questions.prompt: An insurer trains an XGBoost model for 3,000 rounds with no holdout check during training. It scores very well in testing, but its accuracy drops noticeably once it runs on live claims. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The ensemble has too much variance because its trees were trained side by side
The boosted model ran too many rounds and overfit, fitting noise in the training data
Using shallow trees always makes boosting fail on new data
Too few trees were used, so the model still has high bias
questions.why: Boosting mainly reduces bias but overfits if it runs too many rounds without a holdout check, so it can look excellent in testing and then degrade on live data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a random forest and a boosted model like XGBoost each improve on a single decision tree, and name one tradeoff or limit of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: A single decision tree splits the data with yes/no questions on features until it reaches leaves that hold predictions. It is easy to read but unstable and prone to overfitting. A random forest uses bagging: it trains many trees, each on a bootstrap sample (rows drawn with replacement), and each split considers only a random subset of features. Then the trees vote or average. That mainly reduces variance. The tradeoff is that you lose the readability of one tree, and the forest is larger and slower to score. Boosting, as in XGBoost, trains shallow trees one after another. Each tree fits the residual errors left by the earlier ones, scaled by a learning rate. That mainly reduces bias and is often the most accurate choice on tabular data. Its limit is that it can overfit if you run too many rounds, so you need a holdout set to decide when to stop.
rubricPoints: Describes a decision tree as feature splits leading to leaf predictions, chosen by an impurity measure.
Notes that single trees overfit and have high variance.
Explains bagging as training trees on bootstrap samples drawn with replacement and then voting or averaging.
Identifies random-feature selection at each split as what makes a random forest more than plain bagging.
Explains boosting as sequential trees fitted to residuals and scaled by a learning rate.
Names a tradeoff, such as loss of interpretability or boosting's risk of overfitting with too many rounds.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine trains tree models, and the exam tests whether learners can pick bagging, random forest, or boosting for a described situation, so reasoning through scenarios adds the most.

lessons.plain: A neural network is a model built from many small calculators, called neurons, arranged in layers. Each neuron weighs its inputs, adds them up, and decides how strongly to pass a signal on. Training means adjusting those weights a little at a time until the network's answers match known examples. Different layouts suit different data. Some scan images in small patches, some read sequences in order, and some pit two networks against each other to create realistic fakes. Think of a bakery line where every worker tweaks the recipe slightly after tasting the result. The final cake improves through many small corrections that pass back down the line.
lessons.guessPrompt: You need a model that sorts photos of machine parts into 'damaged' and 'fine'. Would a network that scans small patches of the image work better, or one that reads the data one step at a time in order? Why?
lessons.teach:
A neural network is a stack of layers of neurons. Each neuron multiplies its inputs by weights (learned numbers) and adds a bias (a learned offset). It then passes the sum through an activation function, a nonlinear step that lets the network model curves, not just straight lines. ReLU outputs the input if it is positive and zero otherwise, and it is the default for hidden layers. Sigmoid squeezes values to between 0 and 1 for a yes/no output. Tanh squeezes values to between -1 and 1. Softmax turns several scores into probabilities that sum to 1, for multi-class output.

Layer types: a dense (fully connected) layer links every input to every neuron. A convolutional layer slides small filters across a grid to find local patterns such as edges. A pooling layer shrinks that grid. A recurrent layer carries a hidden state from one step of a sequence to the next. Dropout switches off random neurons during training to curb overfitting.

Backpropagation is how the network learns. A forward pass makes a prediction, and a loss scores the error. The calculus chain rule then works backward through the layers to find each weight's gradient, meaning how much the loss changes when that weight changes. Gradient descent moves each weight against its gradient, scaled by a learning rate.

Worked example: one ReLU neuron with input 2, weight 0.5, target 3, and loss (prediction - target) squared. Forward: 2 x 0.5 = 1, ReLU gives 1, loss = 4. Backward: 2 x (1 - 3) = -4, times ReLU slope 1, times input 2, gives a gradient of -8. With learning rate 0.05, the weight becomes 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9. The next prediction is 1.8, which is closer to 3.

Matching architecture to data: CNNs (convolutional networks) suit images. RNNs (recurrent networks) suit sequences such as text or sensor streams. LSTMs are RNNs with gates that keep or forget information, for long-range memory. GANs pair a generator that makes fake samples with a discriminator that tries to catch them. PyTorch and TensorFlow (with its Keras interface) are frameworks that build these layers and compute gradients automatically.

Common mistake: using sigmoid in many hidden layers. Its slope never exceeds 0.25, so gradients shrink layer by layer. This is called a vanishing gradient, and the early layers stop learning.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain trains a single ReLU neuron to predict crates of milk needed. The input is 3, the weight is 0.4, the target is 2, the learning rate is 0.05, and the loss is (prediction - target) squared. Step 1 (forward): 3 x 0.4 = 1.2, and ReLU passes 1.2 through, so the prediction is 1.2 and the loss is (1.2 - 2) squared = 0.64. Step 2 (backward): the loss changes by 2 x (1.2 - 2) = -1.6 per unit of prediction, the ReLU slope is 1 because the sum was positive, and the sum changes by the input for each unit of weight. Step 3: the weight's gradient is ____. Step 4: gradient descent moves the weight against the gradient, giving a new weight of 0.64 and a next prediction of 3 x 0.64 = 1.92, which is closer to 2. What value fills the blank in Step 3?
questions.why: The chain rule multiplies -1.6 by the ReLU slope 1 and by the input 3, giving -4.8, and 0.4 - 0.05 x (-4.8) = 0.64 matches Step 4.

questions.prompt: A water utility wants to forecast pipe pressure from a stream of minute-by-minute sensor readings. Readings from several hours earlier still affect the forecast. Which architecture best fits this problem?
choices: A CNN, because convolutional filters find local patterns such as edges
A GAN, because a generator and discriminator compete to produce samples
A network made only of pooling layers, because pooling shrinks the input
An LSTM, because its gates keep or forget information across a long sequence
questions.why: The data is a sequence that needs long-range memory, and an LSTM is a recurrent network whose gates are built to keep or forget information over many steps.

questions.prompt: A help-desk team builds a network that routes each incoming ticket to exactly one of five departments. Which activation function belongs on the output layer?
choices: ReLU, because it is the default activation for hidden layers
Softmax, because it turns the five scores into probabilities that sum to 1
Tanh, because it squeezes values to between -1 and 1
Sigmoid, because it squeezes each value to between 0 and 1
questions.why: Choosing one class out of several is a multi-class output, and softmax turns several scores into probabilities that sum to 1.

questions.prompt: An engineer builds a 12-layer network that uses sigmoid in every hidden layer. During training, the weights in the last layers change, but the weights in the first few layers barely move at all. What is the most likely cause, and what is a sensible fix?
choices: Vanishing gradients, because sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25 and gradients shrink layer by layer; switch the hidden layers to ReLU
Overfitting, because the network memorises the training data; add dropout to the first layers
A missing bias, because neurons without a bias cannot learn; add a bias to every neuron
Too high a learning rate, because large steps skip over good weights; lower the learning rate
questions.why: Each sigmoid layer multiplies the gradient by a slope of 0.25 or less, so the gradient reaching the early layers is tiny, and ReLU, with a slope of 1 for positive inputs, avoids that shrinking.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how backpropagation trains a network. Say which architecture you would pick for images, for long text sequences, and for generating synthetic data. Name one limit or tradeoff of your choices.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each neuron weighs its inputs, adds a bias, and applies an activation such as ReLU. A forward pass gives a prediction and the loss measures the error. Backpropagation uses the chain rule to work out, from the output backward, how much each weight contributed to that error. Gradient descent then nudges each weight the opposite way, scaled by a learning rate. For images I'd use a CNN, because convolutional filters find local patterns like edges wherever they appear. For long text I'd use an LSTM, whose gates let it remember earlier words that a plain RNN would lose. For synthetic data I'd use a GAN, where a generator learns to fool a discriminator. Tradeoffs: deep networks need lots of data and compute, and GANs can be unstable to train. Sigmoid in deep hidden layers causes vanishing gradients, so I'd keep ReLU there.
rubricPoints: Describes a neuron as weighted inputs plus a bias passed through a nonlinear activation function.
Explains that backpropagation uses the chain rule to compute each weight's gradient, and gradient descent updates the weights.
Matches CNNs to images, RNNs or LSTMs to sequences, and GANs to generating synthetic data.
Notes that LSTM gates address memory loss over long sequences.
Names a real limit, such as vanishing gradients from sigmoid, heavy data and compute needs, or unstable GAN training.

suggested.rationale: The unit's skill is picking the right architecture for a stated problem, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios, plus tracing a backprop step by hand, teaches more than any listed mission or engine, none of which covers neural networks.

lessons.plain: Unsupervised learning means finding patterns in data that has no answer key. Imagine dumping a box of mixed buttons on a table with no instructions: you would naturally sort them into piles by size and color. Clustering does that sorting automatically, and different methods sort in different ways. Some need you to say how many piles you want. Others find piles by how crowded an area is and set aside lonely leftovers. Dimensionality reduction is a second tool. It squeezes data with many measurements down to a few, so you can draw it on a chart or feed it faster to another model. Nearest-neighbor methods work by asking which known examples a new one sits closest to.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have customer data and want to split shoppers into groups, but you have no idea how many groups exist and some customers are strange one-offs. Would you rather use a method that makes you pick the number of groups in advance, or one that finds groups by how tightly packed points are? Why?
lessons.teach:
Unsupervised learning finds structure in data that has no labels, meaning no known right answer for each row. Clustering groups similar rows together.

K-means picks k starting centers called centroids. It assigns each point to its nearest centroid, moves each centroid to the average of the points assigned to it, and repeats until the assignments stop changing. You must choose k up front, and the method favors round clusters of similar size.

Hierarchical clustering, in its common agglomerative form, starts with every point as its own group and keeps merging the two closest groups. It records each merge in a tree diagram called a dendrogram. You cut the tree at some height to get your clusters, so you do not have to fix k beforehand.

DBSCAN (density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise) needs two settings. Epsilon is a radius. The minimum points setting is how many neighbors a point needs within that radius to count as dense. DBSCAN grows clusters outward from dense points and labels points in sparse areas as noise. That lets it find oddly shaped clusters and outliers without being told k.

Dimensionality reduction turns many columns into a few. PCA (principal component analysis) builds new axes called principal components. Each one is a straight-line, or linear, blend of the original columns. They are ordered by how much variance, meaning spread in the data, each one captures. PCA suits compression and preparing data for another model. t-SNE and UMAP are nonlinear methods that keep similar points near each other in 2 or 3 dimensions, and they are mainly used for visualization. UMAP is faster and preserves more of the overall layout. With t-SNE, the gaps between far-apart clusters mean little.

K-nearest neighbors (kNN) is the odd one out because it is actually supervised. It labels a new point by majority vote among the k closest labeled points, or by averaging them when predicting a number.

Here is a worked example of k-means. The points are 1, 2, 9 and 10 on a number line, with k=2 and starting centroids 1 and 2. First assignment: point 1 goes to centroid 1, and points 2, 9 and 10 go to centroid 2. The centroids update to 1 and 7. Second assignment: points 1 and 2 go to centroid 1, and points 9 and 10 go to centroid 7. The centroids update to 1.5 and 9.5. On the next pass nothing moves, so the algorithm stops.

The common mistake is skipping feature scaling. Every method here relies on distance, so a column measured in dollars will swamp one measured in years. In a running system, unscaled inputs quietly produce clusters that reflect units rather than real behavior. Standardize the columns first.

questions.prompt: A courier firm wants to group five delivery stops by their distance from the depot, in kilometres: 2, 4, 20, 22 and 24. It runs k-means with k=2 and starting centroids at 2 and 4. First assignment: stop 2 joins centroid 2, and stops 4, 20, 22 and 24 join centroid 4. Update: the centroids become 2 and 17.5, because (4+20+22+24)/4 = 17.5. Second assignment: stops 2 and 4 join centroid 2, since 4 is 2 km from it but 13.5 km from 17.5. Stops 20, 22 and 24 join centroid 17.5. Update: ???. Third assignment: stops 2 and 4 stay together and stops 20, 22 and 24 stay together, so nothing moves and the algorithm stops. What belongs in the missing update step?
choices: The centroids move to 3 and 22, the averages of {2, 4} and {20, 22, 24}.
The centroids move to 4 and 20, the stops in each group closest to the other group.
The centroids stay at 2 and 17.5, because centroids are fixed once they have been placed.
The algorithm stops here, because every stop is now assigned to a centroid.
questions.why: After each assignment, k-means moves every centroid to the average of the points assigned to it: (2+4)/2 = 3 and (20+22+24)/3 = 22.

questions.prompt: A city transit team has GPS pings from buses. The pings trace long, curving routes, and some stray pings come from faulty sensors. The team does not know how many route groups exist and wants the stray pings flagged rather than forced into a group. Which technique fits best?
choices: K-means, which assigns every ping to the nearest of k centroids
PCA, which reduces the pings to a few principal components
DBSCAN, which grows clusters from dense areas and labels points in sparse areas as noise
K-nearest neighbors, which labels each ping by a vote of its closest neighbors
questions.why: DBSCAN does not need k in advance, can follow oddly shaped clusters, and marks points in sparse areas as noise, which suits the faulty pings.

questions.prompt: A factory logs 300 sensor columns per machine. Before feeding the data into a separate prediction model, an engineer wants to compress it into a smaller set of new columns, ordered by how much of the data's spread each one captures. Which method should the engineer use?
choices: t-SNE, because it keeps similar machines near each other in two dimensions
Hierarchical clustering, because its dendrogram can be cut at any height
UMAP, because it is faster than t-SNE and preserves more of the overall layout
PCA, because it builds linear combinations of the columns ranked by variance captured
questions.why: PCA creates principal components that are linear blends of the original columns, ordered by variance, and it suits compression and preparing data for another model, while t-SNE and UMAP are mainly for visualization.

questions.prompt: An online retailer clusters shoppers using two columns: yearly spend in dollars (roughly 50 to 40,000) and account age in years (roughly 0 to 12). The columns are not scaled. The resulting clusters split shoppers almost entirely by spend. What is the most likely cause, and what is the fix?
choices: Account age has no real effect on behavior, so the clusters are correct as they are
The data has labels, so a supervised method such as k-nearest neighbors should be used instead
The spend column dominates the distance calculation because of its units; standardize both columns first
K is too small; rerun k-means with a larger k until account age matters
questions.why: These methods rely on distance, so a column with large units swamps one with small units, and standardizing the columns stops the clusters from reflecting units instead of behavior.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks: "We have unlabeled sensor data with weird-shaped groups and some junk readings. Should we use k-means, DBSCAN, or kNN, and should we run PCA or t-SNE first?" Explain your choice in your own words, including one limit or tradeoff of what you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use DBSCAN. The data has no labels, so kNN is out, because kNN needs labeled examples to vote. K-means makes us pick the number of clusters and assumes roughly round, even-sized groups, so it would split or merge our odd shapes badly. It would also force every junk reading into some cluster. DBSCAN grows clusters from dense regions, follows irregular shapes, and marks sparse points as noise, which suits the junk readings. The tradeoff is that we must tune epsilon and the minimum-points setting, and it struggles when clusters have very different densities. Before clustering I would standardize the columns, since DBSCAN is distance-based. If there are many columns, PCA is a reasonable linear way to reduce them first. I would use t-SNE or UMAP only to visualize the result, because t-SNE in particular distorts distances between clusters.
rubricPoints: Rules out kNN because it is supervised and needs labels.
Explains that k-means needs k chosen in advance and assumes round, similar clusters.
Explains that DBSCAN uses density, handles odd shapes and labels outliers as noise.
Names a DBSCAN tradeoff, such as tuning epsilon and minimum points or difficulty with uneven densities.
Distinguishes PCA (linear, for preprocessing) from t-SNE or UMAP (nonlinear, mainly for visualization).
Mentions scaling features before any distance-based method.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right unsupervised technique for a described scenario, and no current mission or planned engine covers clustering, so reasoning through situation-based questions adds the most.

lessons.plain: Data science only matters if it helps a business do something better, and it must do so within the rules. In practice that means four things. Compliance is obeying the laws and company policies about data. Privacy means protecting personal details that could identify someone, known as PII. KPIs are the few numbers leaders already watch to judge success. Translating needs means turning a vague request like "sales are down, help" into a precise question a model can answer. Think of a data scientist as an architect. The client describes a feeling ("we need more space"). The architect turns it into a plan that obeys building codes and protects the neighbours' privacy, then measures success in terms the client cares about.
lessons.guessPrompt: A manager says a new churn model is "92% accurate," but leadership asks whether it was worth the money. What single extra piece of information would best answer their question?
lessons.teach:
Data science serves the business, so every project sits inside three constraints and needs one translation step.

Compliance means following the laws, regulations and internal policies that govern data. Two examples are GDPR, the European Union's general privacy law, and HIPAA, the United States law that protects health records.

Privacy focuses on personally identifiable information (PII). PII is any data that can identify a specific person. Some fields do it on their own, such as a name or national ID number. Others do it in combination, such as birth date plus postcode. Common protections include:

Data minimization: collect and keep only the fields the goal needs.
Pseudonymization: replace identifiers with tokens that can be mapped back only with a separately guarded key.
Anonymization: remove identity so it cannot be restored.
Access control: only approved people see raw PII.

A key performance indicator (KPI) is a measurable number the business already uses to judge success. Examples are monthly churn rate and average delivery time.

Translating a business need means turning a vague request into a problem a model can answer. You settle who makes which decision, which KPI should move, what data is allowed, and what result counts as good enough.

Worked example. Marketing says, "We are losing customers; fix it."
Step one: ask which decision this supports. The answer is choosing whom to send a retention offer.
Step two: pick the KPI. Monthly churn rate is currently 4 percent, and the target is 3.5 percent.
Step three: frame the task as classification, which means sorting each customer into one of two groups. Here the model predicts which active customers will cancel within 30 days.
Step four: check compliance. The data includes emails and birth dates, so drop email and convert birth date to an age band. Then confirm customers consented to this use.
Step five: agree how success is measured. Compare churn among contacted customers against a held-out group that received no offer.

A common mistake is reporting only a model metric, such as 92 percent accuracy, without linking it to the KPI. Leaders then cannot tell whether the project helped.

In a running system, skipping the privacy step can expose PII in logs or training sets. That can lead to fines, mandatory breach notifications and lost customer trust.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic network tells its data team, "Too many patients miss appointments; do something." The team works through it. First, the decision: front-desk staff will choose which patients get a personal reminder phone call. Second, the KPI: the no-show rate is currently 15 percent, and the target is 11 percent. Third, the framing: a classification model sorts each upcoming appointment into "likely to be missed" or "likely to be kept." Fourth: [MISSING STEP]. Fifth, success: compare the no-show rate of called patients with a held-out group that received no call. The training data contains patient full names, home phone numbers, diagnosis codes, and appointment history, and the clinic is covered by HIPAA. Which choice best fills the missing fourth step?
choices: Skip any privacy review for now, deploy the model quickly, and anonymize the records later if an auditor raises a concern.
Report the model's accuracy to clinic leaders as the measure of success, since a high accuracy shows the project worked.

Check compliance: remove names and phone numbers from the training set, keep only fields the prediction needs, limit raw-record access to approved staff, and confirm this use of patient data is permitted.
Add more columns, such as patients' employers and insurance numbers, so the model has every available signal and scores higher accuracy.
questions.why: The missing step is the compliance and privacy check: under HIPAA the team must minimize fields, protect identifiers, control access and confirm permitted use before training.

questions.prompt: An online bookstore replaces each customer's account number with a random token such as "C-8841" before giving data to analysts. A separate table linking tokens back to account numbers is locked away, and only the security team can open it. Which privacy protection is this?
choices: Data minimization, because the account number column was reduced to a shorter value.
Pseudonymization, because identifiers are swapped for tokens that can be mapped back only with a separately guarded key.
Anonymization, because analysts can no longer see who the customers are.
A key performance indicator, because each customer now has a measurable code.
questions.why: Tokens that can be reversed with a separately protected key is pseudonymization; anonymization would make restoring identity impossible.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency publishes a ride dataset with no names or card numbers. It does include each rider's exact birth date and home postcode. Why might this dataset still contain PII?
choices: Birth date and postcode together can single out a specific person, so in combination they act as PII.
It cannot contain PII, because PII only means names and national ID numbers.
Ride data is never PII, because it describes trips rather than people.
Postcodes are PII on their own, so only that column needs removing while birth date is safe.
questions.why: PII includes fields that identify a person in combination, and birth date plus postcode can narrow the data down to one individual.

questions.prompt: A logistics company asked its data team to reduce late shipments. Its KPI is the on-time delivery rate, now 88 percent. The team's final report says only, "Our delay-prediction model reached 94 percent precision." What is the main problem with this report?
choices: It gives only a model metric without linking it to the on-time delivery KPI, so leaders cannot tell whether the business improved.
Nothing is wrong, because 94 percent is higher than the 88 percent KPI value, which proves success.
The report should have used a regression model, since classification cannot predict delays.
Precision is the wrong model metric, and the report would be fine if it stated accuracy instead.
questions.why: Reporting a model metric alone, without showing movement in the business KPI, leaves leaders unable to judge whether the project helped.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would take a vague business request and turn it into a data-science project. Cover how KPIs, PII handling and compliance shape the plan, and name one tradeoff that privacy protections can create.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd find the actual decision behind the request, for example choosing which customers get a retention offer. Then I'd tie the project to a KPI the business already tracks, like monthly churn, with a baseline and a target. That way success is judged in business terms, not just model accuracy. Next I'd frame it as a concrete modeling task, such as predicting cancellation within 30 days. Before touching data, I'd check compliance: which laws or policies apply, such as GDPR for EU customers, and whether people consented to this use. For PII I'd practise minimization. I'd drop fields like email, coarsen birth dates into age bands, pseudonymize IDs and restrict raw access. The tradeoff is that removing or coarsening personal fields can cost some predictive power. Anonymized data also can't be linked back for follow-up actions. Still, a slightly weaker model is far better than fines or a breach.
rubricPoints: Starts from the business decision and turns a vague request into a specific modeling question.
Links success to an existing KPI with a baseline and target, not only a model metric.
Defines PII and names concrete protections such as minimization, pseudonymization or access control.
Checks compliance obligations like applicable laws and consent before using data.
Names a tradeoff, such as privacy protections reducing predictive power or traceability.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine covers business framing or PII governance, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios gives the most practice. In those scenarios the learner spots the missing KPI link or privacy control.

lessons.plain: Before any analysis, a data team has to get data, and there are a few ways to do it. You can collect real records as things happen, which is called generated data. You can manufacture realistic fake records, which is called synthetic data. You can study a carefully chosen slice of a huge collection instead of all of it, which is called sampling. Or you can use someone else's dataset, free or paid, under a license. A license is the set of rules saying what you may do with it. Think of stocking a kitchen: you grow some food, buy some, and taste a spoonful rather than the whole pot. You also check the label before reselling anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank wants to train a model to spot fraud, but only 1 in 200 transactions is fraudulent. Besides collecting more real data, what could the team do to give the model enough fraud examples to learn from?
lessons.teach:
Obtaining data means choosing where a dataset comes from and confirming you are allowed to use it that way. Generated data is collected from real activity, such as sensor readings, application logs, survey answers or transactions. It reflects reality, but it can be scarce, slow to gather, or full of personal details. Synthetic data is artificial data that a program produces to imitate the statistical patterns of real data. One way to make it is to draw values from distributions fitted to real records. It helps when real cases are rare, when privacy rules block sharing, or when you need test data. Its limit is that it only holds patterns the generator already captured, so it can miss real-world quirks.

Sampling means analysing a subset of the population, where the population is every record you care about. Teams sample because of cost, speed, storage, or because the full population cannot be reached. In simple random sampling, every record has an equal chance of being picked. In stratified sampling, the population is split into groups called strata, and you sample within each group so that small groups still appear. If a sample does not represent the population, the results carry sampling bias.

Licensing sets the terms of use. Public data, such as government open-data portals, is free to access but often comes with conditions like attribution or no commercial use. Commercial data is bought from a vendor under a contract. That contract may limit redistribution, purpose or duration.

Worked example: a retailer has 10 million return transactions, and 0.5% of them are fraud. Step 1: use the generated transaction logs. Step 2: training on everything is slow, so stratify: keep every fraud case and randomly sample the normal ones. Step 3: fraud examples are still few, so add synthetic fraud records to the training data only, and validate on real held-out data. Step 4: before joining a purchased demographics dataset, confirm the license permits use in a production model.

Common mistake: assuming publicly available means free for any use. In a running system, a model trained on improperly licensed data may have to be withdrawn and retrained, and the company faces legal exposure.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union wants to compare member satisfaction between personal-account and business-account holders. It has 200,000 members, and only 4% (about 8,000) hold business accounts. The budget covers 2,000 surveys. Step 1: The population is defined as all 200,000 members. Step 2: The team decides to sample because surveying every member costs too much. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The selected members are surveyed, and the team compares average satisfaction between the two groups, knowing that both groups contain enough responses to be compared reliably. Which choice best completes Step 3?
choices: Pick 2,000 members by simple random sampling from the whole list, so every member has an equal chance of selection.
Split members into personal and business strata, then randomly select members within each stratum so that the business group is guaranteed enough responses.
Survey the first 2,000 members who visit the website this month, because they are the easiest to reach.
Create 2,000 synthetic survey answers from distributions fitted to last year's results, so no new survey is needed.
questions.why: Stratified sampling draws from each group on purpose, so the small business group is guaranteed enough responses for a reliable comparison, while still keeping random selection within each group.

questions.prompt: A game studio trains a model on player behaviour. It records real click logs from 50,000 players. It also uses a program that draws values from distributions fitted to those logs to create 1 million extra imitation sessions. What is the main limit of the imitation sessions?
choices: They only contain patterns the generator already captured, so they can miss unusual real-world player behaviour.
They are automatically more accurate than the real logs because there are more of them.
They are generated data, so they will always contain personal details about real players.
They cannot be used for training at all, only for testing software.
questions.why: Synthetic data imitates the statistical patterns of real data, so it holds only what the generator captured and can miss real-world quirks.

questions.prompt: A startup downloads a traffic-count dataset from a city's open-data portal. The terms require attribution and forbid commercial use. The startup plans to use it to train a model inside a paid subscription product. What should the team conclude?
choices: The terms only matter if the startup redistributes the raw file, not if it trains a model.
Public data has no conditions, so only commercially purchased data needs a license review.
The data is free to download, so any use is allowed as long as the city is credited.
The planned paid use breaks the no-commercial-use condition, so the team needs different permission or different data before building the model.
questions.why: Publicly available does not mean free for any use; a no-commercial-use condition rules out a paid product, and ignoring it risks withdrawing the model, retraining it and facing legal exposure.

questions.prompt: An online grocer wants to estimate the average order value across all orders placed last year. To save time, an analyst samples only orders placed on Saturdays and Sundays, when large family orders are common. What problem does this create?
choices: No problem, because any subset of the population gives an unbiased estimate if it is large enough.
A synthetic-data problem, because sampled orders are no longer real generated data.
A licensing problem, because the grocer's own transaction logs need a vendor contract.
Sampling bias, because weekend orders do not represent the full population of orders, so the estimate is likely to be too high.
questions.why: When a sample does not represent the population, its results carry sampling bias; weekend-only orders leave out typical weekday orders.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose generated data, synthetic data, sampling, or a licensed external dataset. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Generated data is real activity we collect, like logs or transactions. It is the most faithful to reality, but it can be slow, expensive, scarce for rare events, and loaded with personal information. Synthetic data is fake but statistically realistic. It fills gaps for rare cases or replaces sensitive records, but it only reflects patterns the generator knew, so we should still validate on real data. Sampling lets us work on a subset when the full population is too big or costly to use. Random sampling is simple, while stratified sampling keeps small groups represented. If the sample is not representative, we get biased results. External data saves collection effort. Public datasets may still require attribution or ban commercial use, and commercial datasets come with contract limits on purpose and redistribution. So we check the license before anything reaches production.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes generated data (collected from real activity) from synthetic data (artificially produced to mimic real patterns).
Notes that synthetic data helps with rarity or privacy but should be validated against real data.
Explains why teams sample and that the sample must be representative, mentioning random or stratified sampling.
States that public data is not automatically free for any use and that commercial data has contract restrictions.
Connects licensing violations or bias to a real consequence such as retraining, withdrawal or legal risk.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers data sourcing, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios builds this skill best: spotting a missing sampling, synthetic-data or licensing step in a team's workflow.

lessons.plain: Before a model can learn anything, data has to arrive, be stored in a sensible shape, and be processed on suitable hardware. This objective covers three of those choices. The first is the chips: GPUs (graphics processing units) and TPUs (tensor processing units) do thousands of small calculations at once, which speeds up model training. The second is the file format: CSV is plain rows of text, JSON is nested text records, and Parquet is compressed storage organised by column. The third is orchestration, an automatic scheduler that runs each step of a data pipeline in the right order. Think of a restaurant kitchen: the ovens, the containers, and the head chef who calls each order in sequence.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a table with 50 columns and 10 million rows, and you only need the average of one column. Would you rather the file stored the data row by row or column by column, and why?
lessons.teach:
Data ingestion means bringing data from its sources into your environment. Storage means keeping it in a form that later steps can read efficiently. Three decisions matter here.

Hardware. A CPU (central processing unit) has a few powerful cores that are good at varied, step-by-step work. A GPU has thousands of simpler cores that do the same arithmetic on many numbers at once. Training a neural network is mostly large matrix multiplication, which is exactly that kind of work. A TPU is a chip designed specifically for those tensor (multi-dimensional array) operations. Both speed up training and inference. They cost more and add little for small tabular models or for data cleaning, which a CPU handles well.

File formats. CSV (comma-separated values) is flat text with one row per line. It is easy for people to read and nearly every tool opens it, but it has no built-in schema (declared column types), so dates and numbers can be misread. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is text that allows nested fields, which makes it a good fit for API responses and semi-structured records. It is also verbose. Parquet is a binary, columnar format: it stores each column together, compresses it, and records the schema in the file.

Worked example. The question is the average of one column out of 50, across 10 million rows. With CSV, the reader parses every line, splits all 50 fields, and throws away 49 of them. With Parquet, the reader looks up where that one column sits, reads only that compressed block, and already knows its type. The Parquet job reads far less data and finishes much faster.

Orchestration and automation. An orchestrator such as Apache Airflow describes a pipeline as a DAG (directed acyclic graph). A DAG is a set of tasks with arrows showing which task must finish before the next one starts, and no loops. The orchestrator runs the tasks on a schedule or when a trigger fires, retries tasks that fail, and alerts people when something breaks.

A common mistake is running pipeline steps by hand or with separate timers. If ingestion runs late, the training step still starts and quietly trains on stale or partial data, and the result is a degraded model in production that nobody notices.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic network runs a nightly pipeline in an orchestrator (a tool that runs pipeline tasks in order, on a schedule, with retries and alerts). The pipeline is a DAG, a set of tasks with arrows showing which task must finish before the next starts. The chain is: pull lab results from a partner API, then clean them, then save them as Parquet, then retrain a risk model, then publish the model. Tonight the API pull fails at 1:00 a.m. Trace what happens. Step 1: The orchestrator retries the pull task, as configured. Step 2: The retries also fail, so the pull task is marked failed. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The on-call engineer receives the orchestrator's alert, fixes the API credentials, and reruns the pipeline. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: The orchestrator loops back to the first task and keeps rerunning the whole pipeline until the API responds.
The retrain task still starts at its usual time, using last night's files, so the published model stays reasonably fresh.
The publish task still runs, because it is linked only to the retrain task and not directly to the pull task.
The clean, save, retrain, and publish tasks do not start, because the task upstream of them never finished.
questions.why: In a DAG, each task waits until the tasks pointing into it have finished, so a failed pull blocks everything downstream instead of letting the model train on stale or partial data.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm loads a CSV file of supplier invoices into its analysis tool. Postal codes such as 02134 show up as the number 2134, and some invoice dates are read as plain text instead of dates. Which property of CSV best explains these problems?
choices: CSV stores each column separately and compresses it, which loses leading zeros.
CSV requires nested fields, so flat values such as postal codes get flattened wrongly.
CSV is a binary format, so text values are converted to numbers when it is read.
CSV has no built-in schema, so the reading tool has to guess each column's type.
questions.why: CSV is flat text with no declared column types, so a reader must guess types and can misread values such as postal codes and dates.

questions.prompt: A small insurance analytics team has four workloads and budget to move only one onto rented GPU hardware. A GPU has thousands of simple cores that do the same arithmetic on many numbers at once. Which workload would benefit most?
choices: Fitting a small regression model on 20,000 rows of tabular policy data
Converting a folder of CSV exports into Parquet files each night
Training a neural network that reads photos of vehicle damage, which is mostly large matrix multiplication
Removing duplicate customer records and fixing inconsistent date formats in a 3 GB table
questions.why: Neural-network training is dominated by large matrix multiplication, the same arithmetic on many numbers at once, which is exactly what GPUs speed up, while cleaning, file conversion, and small tabular models run well on a CPU.

questions.prompt: A streaming-music company schedules its ingestion job with one timer at 2:00 a.m. and its model-training job with a separate timer at 4:00 a.m. On busy nights ingestion runs until 5:00 a.m. Over several weeks the recommendation model slowly gets worse, and no one is alerted. Which specific practice is missing?
choices: An orchestrator running the steps as a DAG, so training waits for ingestion to finish and failures trigger alerts
Moving the training job onto TPU hardware so it finishes before the next night's ingestion
Saving the ingested data as JSON instead of CSV so the files can hold nested fields
Starting the training timer one hour later so ingestion normally has more time to finish
questions.why: Separate timers cannot make training wait for ingestion, so the model quietly trains on partial data; an orchestrator with dependencies and alerts fixes the actual cause, while a later timer only shrinks the risk.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why the team might store its large analytical dataset in Parquet and run its pipeline through an orchestrator instead of CSV files and manual scripts. Name one limit or tradeoff of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Parquet stores data by column, compresses it, and keeps the column types inside the file. When we query a few columns of a wide, large table, the reader skips everything else, so jobs read less and run faster. The tradeoff is that Parquet is binary: you can't open it in a text editor, and it is awkward for small files or data that changes row by row. CSV stays handy for small exchanges with people. An orchestrator defines our steps as a dependency graph. It only starts training after ingestion and cleaning succeed, it retries failures, and it alerts us. Without it, a late load can let training run on stale data without anyone noticing. The cost is another system to set up and maintain. Separately, GPUs or TPUs speed up deep-learning training but are expensive and wasted on light tabular work.
rubricPoints: Parquet is columnar, compressed and carries its schema, so analytical queries read only the columns they need.
CSV and JSON are human-readable text and easy to exchange, but they are verbose and CSV lacks enforced types.
An orchestrator runs pipeline tasks as a dependency graph (DAG) with scheduling, retries and alerts.
Without orchestration, steps can run out of order and silently use stale or partial data.
GPUs and TPUs accelerate parallel matrix math for deep learning but add cost and give little benefit for light workloads.
The explanation names at least one concrete tradeoff, such as Parquet not being human-readable or an orchestrator adding operational overhead.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right format, hardware, or orchestration practice for a described workflow, so reasoning through scenario situations builds that judgment best.

lessons.plain: Data wrangling is the cleanup work that turns messy raw data into one consistent table you can analyze. This objective covers three common jobs. Merging lines up two tables that share an ID, such as customers and orders, and combining stacks similar tables on top of each other. Date and time standardization rewrites every timestamp in one agreed format and time zone. Winsorization tames extreme values by pulling them in to a chosen limit instead of throwing them away. Think of preparing ingredients before cooking. You match items from two shopping bags, put every label in the same language, and trim the one giant potato so it cooks evenly with the rest.
lessons.guessPrompt: One office logs a sale at 09:00 New York time and another logs a sale at 10:00 London time on the same day. Which sale actually happened first, and what could go wrong if you simply sorted the raw times as written?
lessons.teach:
Data wrangling is the work of turning raw, inconsistent data into a clean, uniform table. Three techniques come up constantly.

Merging, also called joining, places two datasets side by side by matching a key, which is a column both tables share, such as customer_id. An inner join keeps only the rows whose key appears in both tables. A left join keeps every row of the first table and fills any missing matches with nulls, meaning empty values. Concatenation, also called appending, is a different operation. It stacks datasets that have the same columns on top of each other, such as January sales followed by February sales.

Date/time standardization converts every timestamp to one format and one time zone. The usual format is ISO 8601, which writes year-month-day, for example 2024-03-05T14:00:00Z. The usual zone is UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), a single reference clock. Without this step, 03/05/2024 could mean March 5 or May 3. Local clock times also mislead: 09:00 in New York happens after 10:00 in London on the same day.

Winsorization limits the pull of outliers, which are extreme values. It caps them at chosen percentiles instead of deleting them. A percentile is the value below which a given share of the data falls.

Worked example: ten order amounts sorted are 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 13, 14, 15, 16, 900. Their mean is 101.6. Winsorizing at the 10th and 90th percentiles caps the bottom tenth and top tenth of the values. With ten values, that means the lowest value (10) becomes the next value up, 11, and the highest (900) becomes the next value down, 16. The new mean is 13.3, and all ten rows are kept.

A common mistake is joining on a key that repeats in one table. For example, a customer table might list the same ID twice. Each matching order then appears twice, which silently multiplies rows. In a running system this inflates revenue totals and feeds duplicated records into model training, so always check that keys are unique and that row counts make sense before and after a merge.

questions.prompt:
A weather station logs ten wind-speed readings (km/h), sorted: 3, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38. One reading of 3 came from a sensor that briefly stuck. The analyst winsorizes at the 10th and 90th percentiles, which means capping the bottom tenth and the top tenth of the values. Winsorization limits the pull of outliers, which are extreme values, by capping them at chosen percentiles. A percentile is the value below which a given share of the data falls.

Step 1: With ten values, the bottom tenth is the single lowest value (3) and the top tenth is the single highest value (38).
Step 2: The lowest value, 3, is changed to: ____
Step 3: The highest value, 38, is replaced by the next value down, 37.
Step 4: All ten rows are kept, and the extreme low reading no longer drags the mean down as much.

What goes in Step 2?
choices: 30, the next value up in the sorted list
It stays at 3, because winsorization only caps unusually high values
It is deleted, leaving nine readings in the dataset
34.9, the mean of all ten readings
questions.why: Winsorization caps the lowest tenth by replacing it with the next value up, so 3 becomes 30 and no row is removed.

questions.prompt: A veterinary chain keeps a separate appointments table for each of its four clinics. All four tables have exactly the same columns: appointment_id, pet_name, date and fee. The analyst wants one table that lists every appointment from all four clinics. Which operation fits?
choices: An inner join on appointment_id, keeping only appointments found in all four tables
A left join on pet_name, keeping the first clinic's rows and filling the rest with nulls
Winsorization of the fee column, capping the extreme values
Concatenation (appending): stack the four tables on top of each other
questions.why: Concatenation stacks datasets with the same columns, so the rows from all four clinics end up in one table; a join would instead match rows side by side on a shared key.

questions.prompt: A shipping company combines scan logs from its Sydney and Toronto depots. Both depots record times like "04/06/2024 08:15" in their own local time. Analysts want to know which scan happened first. What should they do first?
choices: Sort the rows by the raw text so that the earlier-looking clock times come first
Convert every timestamp to ISO 8601 (year-month-day) format in UTC, a single reference clock
Join the two logs on the timestamp column with an inner join
Winsorize the timestamps so that unusually early or late scans are capped
questions.why: Converting to one format and one time zone settles whether 04/06 means April 6 or June 4, and it puts both depots' scans on the same clock so they can be compared.

questions.prompt: A retailer runs a left join of its 8,000-row sales table (the first table) to a products table on product_id. Afterward, the result has 8,900 rows, and total revenue looks higher than last month's report. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Winsorization was applied to revenue before the join
The left join dropped sales whose product_id was missing from the products table
Some product_id values appear more than once in the products table, so their matching sales were duplicated
The timestamps were not converted to UTC before the merge
questions.why: A key that repeats in one table makes every matching row appear more than once, which inflates the row count and revenue; a left join on its own keeps every sales row but never adds extra rows.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would merge, standardize timestamps, and winsorize a sales dataset before modeling, and name one tradeoff or limit of winsorization.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I would merge orders with the customer table on customer_id. I'd use a left join if I need to keep every order even when customer details are missing. I would check that customer_id is unique in the customer table and compare row counts before and after, because duplicate keys silently multiply rows. If I'm adding new months of orders with the same columns, that is concatenation, not a join. Next I would convert every timestamp to ISO 8601 in UTC, so ambiguous dates like 03/05 and different local time zones can't scramble the order of events. Finally I would winsorize order amounts, for example capping them at the 1st and 99th percentiles, so a few huge orders don't dominate the mean. The tradeoff is that winsorizing changes real values.
