If those extreme orders are genuine and matter, such as for fraud detection, capping hides exactly the signal I need.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes a join on a shared key from concatenation that stacks tables with the same columns.
Mentions checking key uniqueness or row counts to avoid duplicated rows after a merge.
States that timestamps should use one format such as ISO 8601 and one zone such as UTC.
Describes winsorization as capping extremes at percentiles rather than deleting rows.
Names a limit, such as distorting genuine extreme values or choosing percentile cutoffs arbitrarily.

suggested.rationale: The unit asks learners to spot which wrangling step a team's workflow is missing, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios with duplicated joins, mixed time zones and outlier-skewed means builds that skill best.

lessons.plain: Data science projects follow a repeatable path from a business question to a working model, and teams use habits that keep that path organized. CRISP-DM is a well-known map of that path. Its name stands for Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining, and it splits a project into six phases that loop back on each other. Version control is a system that records every change to code and files so you can see who changed what and undo mistakes. Clean code means writing programs that others can read, rerun and trust. Think of a recipe book: CRISP-DM is the order of the steps, version control is the edit history, and clean code is legible handwriting.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team builds a model that scores well in testing, but six months later nobody can rebuild it because the notebook was edited many times and the data file was overwritten. What kind of habit or tool would have prevented this?
lessons.teach:
CRISP-DM (Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining) is a workflow model, meaning a named sequence of project phases. It has six phases. Business understanding defines the goal and how success will be measured. Data understanding collects and explores the data. Data preparation cleans and shapes it. Modeling trains candidate models. Evaluation checks whether the model meets the business goal, not just a statistical score. Deployment puts it into use. The phases are iterative: findings in one phase often send you back to an earlier one, which is why the model is drawn as a cycle.

Version control is a system, Git being the common example, that stores snapshots called commits, each with a message and author. Branches let people work on separate copies and merge them later. In data science you should also version the data and the trained model (the saved artifact), so any result can be traced to exact code, data and settings.

Clean code is code that is readable and reproducible: descriptive names, small single-purpose functions, no hard-coded file paths or passwords, settings kept in a config file, a fixed random seed so results repeat, and automated tests.

Worked example: a churn team trains a model with 91% accuracy. Step 1, in evaluation they notice the business wanted to catch high-value customers, which the model misses. Step 2, they return to business understanding and data preparation to add spend features. Step 3, each change is committed with a message, and the dataset version is recorded. Step 4, when a later run drops to 85%, they compare commits and find a renamed column broke a feature.

A common mistake is treating CRISP-DM as a one-way checklist and skipping evaluation against business goals, or versioning code but not data. In a running system, that means a deployed model nobody can reproduce, audit or safely roll back.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency wants to predict bus delays. The work so far: (1) Business understanding: the goal is fewer missed transfers, so success means flagging at least 80% of delays longer than 5 minutes at the 12 transfer hubs. (2) Data understanding: the team explores GPS logs and finds weekend records are sparse. (3) Data preparation: they fill gaps and build features for time of day and route. (4) Modeling: the best candidate scores an R-squared of 0.88 across all stops. (5) ??? (6) Deployment follows only after step 5 is satisfied. Which action belongs in step 5?
choices: Check whether it flags 80% of hub delays over 5 minutes; it flags only 58%, so loop back to earlier phases.
Commit the final training script to Git and overwrite the old GPS file with the cleaned version.
Tune hyperparameters until R-squared reaches 0.95, then treat the model as ready for deployment.
Deploy the model now, because an R-squared of 0.88 already shows it is strong enough for live use.
questions.why: Evaluation judges the model against the business success measure set in business understanding, not just a statistical score, and a shortfall sends the team back to an earlier phase.

questions.prompt: A lending team keeps all its Python code in Git with clear commit messages. Each week, though, it overwrites a single training file called loans.csv and saves the retrained model over the previous one. Six months later an auditor asks why the model approved a particular applicant in March. What practice is the team missing?
choices: Writing longer, more descriptive commit messages for the code changes
Versioning the training data and the saved model artifact alongside the code
Splitting the code into more branches so each analyst has a separate copy
Adding automated tests to check that each function returns the expected type
questions.why: Without versioned data and model artifacts, nobody can trace the March result to the exact data and model that produced it, even if the code is versioned.

questions.prompt: An analyst at a grocery chain runs the same forecasting script twice, on the same data and the same code, and gets 73% accuracy the first time and 76% the second. The script also contains a hard-coded path to her laptop and some variables named x1 and tmp. Which clean-code change directly fixes the fact that the results do not repeat?
choices: Rename x1 and tmp to descriptive names
Move the laptop file path into a config file
Set a fixed random seed in the script
Create a new Git branch before each run
questions.why: A fixed random seed makes random steps, such as data splits, come out the same every run, so results repeat. The other changes improve readability or portability but not repeatability.

questions.prompt: An insurance company's data team holds a meeting to agree that its fraud project's goal is to cut fraudulent claim payouts by 10% within a year, and that this figure is how success will be judged. In CRISP-DM, which phase is this?
choices: Data understanding
Data preparation
Business understanding
Evaluation
questions.why: Business understanding is the phase that defines the project goal and how success will be measured. Evaluation later checks the model against that measure.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how CRISP-DM, version control and clean code fit together on a data science project, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on them.
lessons.modelAnswer: CRISP-DM gives us the project's phases: business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modeling, evaluation and deployment. It is a loop, so if evaluation shows the model misses the business goal, we go back and rework earlier phases. Version control records every change as a commit, so we can compare runs, work on branches and roll back. For data science we should version the data and saved model too, not just code, or we cannot reproduce results. Clean code, meaning clear names, small functions, config files instead of hard-coded values, fixed random seeds and tests, makes the work readable and repeatable by others. The tradeoff is overhead: these practices take time and discipline, and CRISP-DM itself does not cover operational details like monitoring a deployed model, so it needs MLOps practices alongside it.
rubricPoints: Names the six CRISP-DM phases or most of them in order.
States that CRISP-DM is iterative, not a one-way sequence.
Explains version control as tracked, reversible changes via commits and branches.
Notes that data and models should be versioned as well as code for reproducibility.
Describes clean-code habits such as clear names, config files, fixed seeds and tests.
Names a limit, such as process overhead or CRISP-DM not covering ongoing operations.

suggested.rationale: The exam asks learners to spot which life-cycle phase or practice a described team is missing, so reasoning through scenario situations builds that skill best.

lessons.plain: DevOps is a way of working where the people who write software and the people who run it share automated, repeatable steps for shipping changes safely. MLOps applies the same habits to machine learning, where what you ship is a trained model plus the data and code behind it. Think of a restaurant kitchen: recipes are tested before going on the menu (automated testing), every dish leaves in a standard container (packaging), a manager assigns cooks as orders spike (orchestration), and someone tastes plates all night to catch a dish going off (monitoring). Skip any one and quality slips quietly.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model predicted customer churn very accurately on launch day, and its server has never crashed since. Six months later the business says its predictions are poor. What could have gone wrong, and how might the team have noticed sooner?
lessons.teach:
DevOps joins development and operations through automation so changes reach users quickly and safely. MLOps extends it to machine learning, where the shipped item is a model plus its training data and code. CI/CD means continuous integration and continuous delivery (or deployment). CI automatically builds and tests every change. CD packages the result and moves it toward production through repeatable steps. In MLOps the pipeline also validates incoming data, retrains the model, and compares the new model's metrics with the current one before promoting it. Model deployment puts a trained model where it can make predictions. That can be batch scoring, which runs on a schedule, or a real-time endpoint, which is an API answering requests. A container bundles the model, its code, and exact library versions so it runs the same everywhere. Container orchestration is software, Kubernetes being the common example, that places containers across machines, restarts failed ones, and scales copies with load. Performance monitoring watches a live model in two ways. Technical health covers latency and error rates. Model health covers data drift (inputs shift away from the training data), concept drift (the link between inputs and the correct answer changes), and accuracy once true labels arrive.

These practices work because automation removes manual steps that can't be repeated, containers remove environment differences, and monitoring catches decay that no pre-release test can foresee.

Worked example: a fraud model is trained in a notebook and emailed to operations. First, nobody tests the training code, so a bug ships; the missing practice is CI. Second, operations installs libraries by hand and a version mismatch changes the scores; the missing practice is containerization. Third, holiday traffic overwhelms one server; the missing practice is orchestration with autoscaling. Fourth, fraud patterns change and recall falls without anyone noticing; the missing practice is drift monitoring tied to a retraining trigger.

Common mistake: monitoring only uptime and latency. A model can return fast, valid responses that are increasingly wrong. In a running system the result is silent business loss until someone notices the outcomes.

questions.prompt: A ride-share company runs a fare-pricing model as a real-time endpoint, which is an API that answers each price request as it arrives. An engineer reviews three problems and names the missing practice for each. Problem 1: a developer changed the feature code, nothing checked it automatically, and a broken feature reached production. Missing practice: CI (continuous integration, which automatically builds and tests every change). Problem 2: the model scored differently on the staging server than on the production server because the two machines had different library versions. Missing practice: containerization (bundling the model, code and exact library versions so it runs the same everywhere). Problem 3: the company launches in a new outer suburb. Requests now show an average trip distance about 40% longer than anything in the training data. Latency and error rates look normal, and the true outcomes for these trips will not be known for 30 days. Which missing practice should the engineer name for Problem 3?
choices: Data drift monitoring on the model's inputs, because incoming requests are moving away from the training data
Latency and error-rate monitoring, because these are the first signs of a failing model
Concept drift monitoring, because the link between trip features and the correct fare has been shown to have changed
Container orchestration with autoscaling, because the new suburb adds request load
questions.why: The inputs themselves have shifted away from the training data, and that is data drift. It can be detected right away, without waiting 30 days for true outcomes, and latency monitoring would miss it because technical health looks fine.

questions.prompt: An insurer's claim-approval model gets inputs with the same patterns as always: similar claim amounts, regions and policy types. A new regulation, however, changes which of those claims should correctly be approved. The model's accuracy falls once true decisions come back. What is this called?
choices: Concept drift, because the link between the inputs and the correct answer has changed
Data drift, because the inputs have moved away from the training data
A technical health failure, because accuracy is a latency measure
A container version mismatch, because the model now behaves differently
questions.why: The inputs are unchanged, but the right answer for those same inputs has changed. That shift in the input-to-answer relationship is the definition of concept drift.

questions.prompt: A streaming service's MLOps pipeline retrains its churn-prediction model every Sunday and automatically replaces the live model with the new one. One week the retrained model is noticeably worse, and it goes live anyway. Which specific practice is the pipeline missing?
choices: Batch scoring, so predictions run on a schedule instead of in real time
Container orchestration, so failed copies of the model restart automatically
Uptime monitoring, so the team knows the endpoint is responding
A step that compares the new model's metrics with the current model's before promoting it
questions.why: In MLOps, the delivery pipeline should check a retrained model's metrics against the current one and promote it only if it holds up. Here that gate is missing, so a worse model shipped.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop's recommendation model has a monitoring dashboard showing 99.9% uptime, 80 ms average latency and almost no errors. Over two months, though, purchases from recommended titles fell by a quarter, and nobody was alerted. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
choices: The team needs continuous integration, because the dashboard proves the training code has a bug
The model should switch to batch scoring, because real-time endpoints cannot be monitored for accuracy
The endpoint needs container orchestration, because 80 ms latency means the servers are overloaded
The team is monitoring only technical health. It also needs model health monitoring: drift checks and accuracy once true outcomes arrive
questions.why: Fast, valid responses can still be increasingly wrong. Watching only uptime and latency hides model decay, which leads to silent business loss like this drop in purchases.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how CI/CD, containers, orchestration, and monitoring each protect a deployed model, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on them.
lessons.modelAnswer: CI/CD automates the path from a code or data change to production. CI runs tests and data checks on every change. CD packages the model and promotes it only if it beats the current one on agreed metrics. Containers freeze the model with its exact libraries, so it predicts the same on a laptop and in production. Orchestration such as Kubernetes runs many container copies, replaces crashed ones, and scales with traffic. Monitoring watches latency and errors, but also data drift, concept drift, and real accuracy once labels arrive. That matters because a healthy server can still serve a decaying model. One tradeoff is that accuracy monitoring depends on ground-truth labels, which often arrive weeks late. So teams lean on drift signals as early warnings, and those can raise false alarms. All this automation also adds setup and maintenance cost.
rubricPoints: CI automatically tests changes and CD repeatably promotes them, including a model-versus-current comparison in MLOps.
Containers package the model with its dependencies so it behaves identically across environments.
Orchestration schedules, restarts, and scales containers across machines.
Monitoring covers both technical health and model health, meaning drift and accuracy.
Names a real limit, such as delayed labels, drift false alarms, or added complexity.

suggested.rationale: The unit's mastery goal is spotting which specific MLOps practice a described workflow lacks, so reasoning through exam-style team scenarios adds the most.

lessons.plain: A deployment environment is the place where a finished model actually runs and does its work. There are four common choices. On-premises means machines your organization owns, in its own building. Cloud means renting computing from a provider over the internet. Hybrid mixes the two, keeping some parts in-house and some rented. Edge means running the model on or near the device that produces the data, such as a camera, a vehicle or a factory sensor. Think of where to cook a meal: your own kitchen, a rented commercial kitchen, a mix of both, or a grill right beside the guests so the food arrives hot and fast.
lessons.guessPrompt: A factory wants a model to spot defects on a conveyor belt and stop the line within a few milliseconds, and the factory's internet link sometimes drops. Where would you run the model, and why?
lessons.teach:
A deployment environment is the location and infrastructure where a trained model receives inputs and returns predictions. The choice depends on a few factors. Latency is the delay between sending data and getting an answer. Data residency means rules about where data is allowed to be stored or processed. Elasticity is the ability to add or remove computing capacity quickly as demand changes. Capital expense means paying up front for equipment you own. Operating expense means paying as you go for what you use.

On-premises gives full control over hardware and data, which helps with strict residency or security rules, but it costs capital up front, scales slowly, and your team maintains everything. Cloud offers elasticity, on-demand GPUs and managed services billed as operating expense, but data leaves your building, network dependence is total, and costs can grow if usage is not watched. Hybrid keeps sensitive data or steady workloads on-premises while sending bursty work such as large training jobs to the cloud. It gives flexibility at the cost of more complexity in networking, security and keeping two environments consistent. Edge runs inference on or near the data source. It gives very low latency, works offline and sends less raw data over the network, but devices have limited memory and power, so models often must be shrunk, and updating thousands of devices is hard.

Worked example: a hospital trains an imaging model. Step one, the patient scans fall under residency rules, so storage and inference stay on-premises. Step two, training needs many GPUs for a few days each quarter. Buying them would leave them idle most of the year, so training on anonymized data bursts to the cloud. Step three, that combination is hybrid.

A common mistake is assuming cloud is always the answer. If a self-driving cart must react in milliseconds, a round trip to a distant data center is too slow and fails whenever the link drops. In a running system, that wrong choice shows up as missed real-time decisions or as compliance violations.

questions.prompt: A farm-equipment maker wants its tractors to spot weeds in camera images and decide in a fraction of a second whether to spray. Fields often have no mobile signal. The team reasons it through in three steps. Step one: the spray decision must happen almost instantly and keep working with no network, so inference runs on a small computer mounted on each tractor. That is an edge deployment (running predictions on or near where the data is created). Step two: MISSING. Step three: once a month, tractors back at the depot upload a sample of images, and the larger model is retrained on rented cloud computing capacity before the updated, smaller version is pushed back to the fleet. Which statement correctly fills in step two?
choices: The company should buy a rack of on-premises servers for each field so the tractors can reach them over a local cable.
Because edge inference is local, the tractor computer has no meaningful limits, so the full-size training model can be copied onto it unchanged.
Each tractor should stream every camera frame to a cloud data center and wait for the spray decision to come back.
The tractor computer has limited memory and power, so the model must be shrunk to a smaller version that fits and runs fast enough on the device.
questions.why: Edge devices have limited memory and power, so a model running on them usually has to be made smaller, which is exactly the step between choosing edge and retraining the larger model elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A data-science team says it needs an environment with high elasticity. Which description matches what elasticity means?
choices: Keeping the time between sending a request and getting a prediction as short as possible
Following rules about which country or building data may be stored or processed in
Paying for all equipment up front so that it is fully owned by the company
Being able to add or remove computing capacity quickly as demand rises and falls
questions.why: Elasticity is the ability to scale computing capacity up or down quickly as demand changes; the other choices describe latency, data residency and capital expense.

questions.prompt: A three-person startup runs a recipe-recommendation model. Its traffic is tiny most weeks but jumps twentyfold when a cooking show mentions it. It has no data-residency rules, no spare money to buy servers, and no staff to maintain hardware. Predictions within a second or two are fine. Which deployment environment fits best?
choices: Edge, because running the model on users' phones gives the lowest latency
Cloud, because it scales up for spikes, is billed as you go, and the provider manages the infrastructure
Hybrid, because splitting the work across two environments is always safer
On-premises, because owning the hardware gives full control over the data
questions.why: Unpredictable spikes, no residency limits, no upfront budget and no maintenance staff all point to the cloud's elasticity, operating-expense billing and managed services.

questions.prompt: An insurer scores claims on its own on-premises servers and sends occasional large retraining jobs to the cloud. After a retrain, the model produces different scores on-premises than it did in the cloud, because the two environments are running different versions of the same software libraries. Which known drawback of this deployment choice does this show?
choices: Cloud costs grow when usage is not watched, which changed the model's outputs
Edge devices have limited memory, so the model was automatically shrunk and lost accuracy
Hybrid setups add the work of keeping two environments consistent, and drift between them causes mismatched behavior
On-premises hardware scales slowly, so the servers could not handle the claim volume
questions.why: Combining on-premises and cloud is a hybrid deployment, and one of its costs is the effort of keeping both environments in step; the version mismatch is exactly that failure.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between on-premises, cloud, hybrid and edge deployment for a model, and name one tradeoff each option forces you to accept.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the constraints, not the technology. If the model must answer in milliseconds or keep working when the network is down, I put inference at the edge, on or near the device. The tradeoff is small hardware, so I may need a compressed model, and pushing updates to many devices is harder. If rules say data cannot leave our site, or we need full control, I choose on-premises. The tradeoff is up-front hardware cost and slow scaling. If demand is bursty or we need lots of GPUs briefly, cloud gives elasticity and pay-as-you-go billing. The tradeoffs are network dependence, data leaving our premises and costs that can creep up. When different parts have different needs, such as sensitive inference in-house and heavy training rented, hybrid fits. Its tradeoff is the added complexity of running and securing two environments consistently.
rubricPoints: Defines each of the four environments by where the model runs.
Links edge to low latency, offline operation and constrained devices.
Links on-premises to control and data residency but up-front cost and slow scaling.
Links cloud to elasticity and pay-as-you-go but network dependence and cost growth.
Describes hybrid as splitting workloads, with added operational complexity as the tradeoff.
Chooses based on requirements such as latency, residency and demand pattern rather than defaulting to one option.

suggested.rationale: This objective is tested by matching a scenario's latency, residency and scaling constraints to the right environment, so reasoning through exam-style situations builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Optimization means picking the best choice by some score, like the lowest cost or highest profit. Sometimes you can pick anything (unconstrained); usually there are rules, like a budget or limited machine time, that a valid answer must obey (constrained). A multi-armed bandit is a special repeated-choice problem: picture a row of slot machines with unknown payouts. Each pull teaches you something, but every pull spent testing a poor machine costs you winnings. You must balance trying machines to learn about them against sticking with the one that looks best so far.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website has five headline versions and wants to earn the most clicks while still testing them. Would you split visitors evenly among all five until next month, or gradually send more visitors to whichever headline seems to be winning? Why?
lessons.teach:
Optimization means choosing values for decision variables (the things you control) to make an objective function (the single number a choice is scored by, such as profit, cost or model error) as large or as small as possible.

Unconstrained optimization lets the decision variables take any value. Training a regression model by gradient descent is the classic case: you repeatedly nudge the weights in the direction that lowers the loss (the error measure), and no weight value is forbidden. Constrained optimization adds constraints, which are rules a valid answer must obey, such as a budget cap, a capacity limit or no negative quantities. Answers obeying every constraint are called feasible. Linear programming solves constrained problems whose objective and constraints are all linear (straight-line); Lagrange multipliers are a calculus method that folds equality constraints into the objective.

Worked example: maximize profit 5x + 4y. Product x uses 2 machine hours, y uses 1, only 100 hours exist, and at most 60 units of y can sell. Without constraints profit grows forever, so there is no meaningful answer. With 2x + y ≤ 100, y ≤ 60 and x, y ≥ 0, check the corners: (50, 0) gives 250, (20, 60) gives 340, (0, 60) gives 240. The best feasible plan is x = 20, y = 60.

A multi-armed bandit problem is a repeated choice among options (arms) whose payoffs are unknown and learned only by trying them. The tension is exploration (trying arms to learn) versus exploitation (picking the best-looking arm). Epsilon-greedy picks a random arm a small fraction epsilon of the time, say 10%, and the best-so-far arm otherwise. Upper confidence bound (UCB) favours arms that look promising or are under-tested; Thompson sampling picks each arm in proportion to its estimated chance of being best. Unlike a fixed A/B test that splits traffic evenly until the end, a bandit shifts traffic toward winners while still learning, losing less reward along the way.

Common mistake: a purely greedy bandit (epsilon of zero). One lucky early result locks traffic onto a weaker arm and the better arm is never measured, so a live recommendation or pricing system quietly earns less indefinitely.

questions.prompt: A small bakery wants to maximize profit 3a + 2b, where a is trays of bagels and b is trays of muffins. A bagel tray uses 1 kg of flour and a muffin tray uses 2 kg; only 40 kg of flour are available, so a + 2b ≤ 40. The oven can fit at most 20 bagel trays, so a ≤ 20. Trays cannot be negative, so a, b ≥ 0. The bakery checks the corners of the feasible region: (0, 0) gives 0, (20, 0) gives 60, and (0, 20) gives 40. The remaining corner is (20, 10), where flour use is 20 + 2(10) = 40, exactly the limit. What is the missing step that finishes the problem?
choices: (20, 10) gives 3(20) + 2(10) = 80, the highest corner, so the best feasible plan is 20 bagel trays and 10 muffin trays.
Profit 3a + 2b has no upper limit, so the bakery should bake as many trays of both as it can.
(20, 10) gives 60, the same as (20, 0), so either plan is equally good.
(0, 20) is best because muffins use more flour, so they must be the more valuable product.
questions.why: The point (20, 10) obeys every constraint, and its profit of 80 beats every other corner, so it is the best feasible plan.

questions.prompt: A courier firm wants to choose routes that make total fuel cost as small as possible. Each van carries at most 800 kg, every parcel must be delivered, and no van may work more than 9 hours. Which kind of optimization problem is this?
choices: Constrained optimization, because valid route plans must obey capacity, delivery and time rules
A fixed A/B test, because two route plans should be compared with an even split
A multi-armed bandit problem, because the firm chooses among many routes
Unconstrained optimization, because fuel cost is a single number to minimize
questions.why: The limits on load, deliveries and hours are constraints a valid answer must obey, which makes this a constrained optimization problem.

questions.prompt: A news website has five candidate headlines for a story and does not know which one gets the most clicks. It wants to learn click rates from live readers while losing as few clicks as possible during the test. Which approach best fits?
choices: Linear programming, because the headline choice is an objective with linear constraints
A fixed A/B-style test that splits readers evenly across all five headlines until the end
A multi-armed bandit, such as Thompson sampling, that shifts readers toward winning headlines while still testing the others
Gradient descent, nudging each headline's text in the direction that lowers error
questions.why: The payoffs are unknown and learned only by trying each headline, and a bandit moves traffic toward winners as it learns, losing less reward than an even split.

questions.prompt: A mobile game studio uses a bandit to pick which of three in-game offers to show players, with epsilon set to 0. On day one, offer B happens to get a few lucky purchases and pulls ahead. What is the most likely long-term result?
choices: Traffic is split evenly across all three offers until the test ends, like an A/B test.
Offer B keeps being shown almost always, the other offers are rarely or never measured again, and if one of them is actually better the studio quietly earns less indefinitely.
The bandit eventually tries offers A and C at random 10% of the time and corrects itself.
The bandit behaves like Upper confidence bound and favours the under-tested offers.
questions.why: With epsilon of zero the bandit is purely greedy and never explores, so an early lucky arm locks in and a better arm is never discovered.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between constrained and unconstrained optimization, and when a multi-armed bandit beats a classic A/B test. Name one limit or tradeoff of the bandit approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Optimization is choosing the inputs that maximize or minimize an objective, like profit or model error. In unconstrained optimization any input value is allowed, as when gradient descent tunes model weights to lower loss. In constrained optimization the answer must respect limits such as budget, capacity or non-negativity, so we only consider feasible solutions, often using linear programming or Lagrange multipliers. A multi-armed bandit is for repeated choices among options with unknown payoffs: it balances exploring options to learn against exploiting the current best. Methods like epsilon-greedy, UCB or Thompson sampling shift traffic toward winners during the test, so it loses less reward than an even A/B split. The tradeoff is that because traffic is uneven and adaptive, you get less clean evidence about the weaker options, and if you explore too little you can lock onto a lucky but worse arm.
rubricPoints: Defines optimization as maximizing or minimizing an objective over decision variables.
Unconstrained allows any values; constrained must satisfy limits and stay feasible.
Names a method for each, such as gradient descent versus linear programming or Lagrange multipliers.
Describes a bandit as repeated choice under uncertainty balancing exploration and exploitation.
Contrasts a bandit with a fixed A/B test: adaptive traffic means less lost reward.
Names a tradeoff, such as weaker evidence about losing arms or getting stuck with too little exploration.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers optimization or bandits, and the exam rewards recognizing from a scenario whether constraints exist or an explore-exploit bandit fits, so reasoning through exam-style situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: Natural language processing, or NLP, is how computers work with human language such as reviews, emails, and contracts. Computers only handle numbers, so NLP first chops text into small pieces, then turns those pieces into numbers that capture which words matter or what they mean. With that done, a system can tell whether a review is happy or angry, pull out names of people and companies, find the main themes in thousands of documents, or write new sentences. Think of it like a librarian who first sorts every book into words, then indexes them, and only then can answer questions about the whole library.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you wanted a computer to decide which words best describe one support ticket out of a hundred, would a word like "the" or a word like "refund" be more useful, and why?
lessons.teach:
Natural language processing (NLP) is the set of techniques that turn human text into numbers a model can use, then perform tasks with them. Tokenization comes first. It splits raw text into units called tokens, which may be whole words, word pieces (subwords), or characters. A word embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) learned for each token so that words used in similar contexts land close together, so "car" sits near "truck". TF-IDF (term frequency-inverse document frequency) is a simpler weighting. Term frequency counts how often a word appears in one document. Inverse document frequency shrinks words that appear in many documents. Their product is high for words common in this document but rare elsewhere. Topic modeling, for example latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA), is unsupervised, meaning it needs no labels. It finds groups of words that tend to appear together and treats each group as a theme.

Worked example: take 100 support tickets. In ticket A, "the" appears 5 times and "refund" 3 times. "The" appears in all 100 tickets, so its IDF is log10(100/100) = 0 and its score is 5 x 0 = 0. "Refund" appears in 10 tickets, so its IDF is log10(100/10) = 1 and its score is 3 x 1 = 3. TF-IDF correctly flags ticket A as being about refunds.

Applications build on these steps. Sentiment analysis labels text as positive, negative, or neutral, as with product reviews. Named entity recognition (NER) tags spans of text as people, organizations, places, dates, or amounts, such as company names in contracts. Text generation repeatedly predicts the next token to write new text, as chatbots and summarizers do.

A common mistake is treating TF-IDF as understanding meaning. It ignores word order and synonyms, so "not good" resembles "good", and "car" looks unrelated to "automobile". Embeddings capture similarity better. In a running system, production must tokenize exactly as training did. Otherwise the model receives tokens it never learned, and accuracy quietly drops.

questions.prompt: A news site has 1,000 articles and wants to know what article X is about using TF-IDF with log base 10. In article X, "said" appears 6 times and "vaccine" appears 3 times. Step 1: "said" appears in all 1,000 articles, so its IDF is log10(1000/1000) = 0 and its score is 6 x 0 = 0. Step 2: "vaccine" appears in only 10 of the 1,000 articles, so its IDF is ______. Step 3: its score is 3 x 2 = 6, so TF-IDF flags article X as being about vaccines. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: 1000/10 = 100, the raw ratio of total articles to articles with the word
log10(10/1000) = -2, because the word is rare
log10(1000/3) ≈ 2.52, using the count of the word in article X
questions.why: IDF is the log of total documents divided by the number of documents that contain the word, so log10(1000/10) = log10(100) = 2, which matches the score of 3 x 2 = 6 in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A shipping company receives thousands of freight invoices as plain text. It wants software that automatically marks which parts of each invoice are company names, city names, delivery dates and dollar amounts. Which NLP technique fits this task?
choices: Topic modeling with LDA
Text generation
Sentiment analysis
Named entity recognition (NER)
questions.why: NER tags spans of text as people, organizations, places, dates or amounts, which is exactly what labeling company names, cities, dates and dollar figures requires.

questions.prompt: A hospital's internal search tool scores documents with TF-IDF. Staff complain that searching for "physician" misses notes that only say "doctor". Which change most directly addresses this?
choices: Run topic modeling so that every note receives a sentiment label
Represent words with word embeddings, which place words used in similar contexts close together
Remove the inverse document frequency part so common words are not shrunk
Raise the term frequency weight so repeated words count more
questions.why: TF-IDF treats different words as unrelated even when they mean the same thing, while embeddings learn vectors that put similar words like "physician" and "doctor" near each other.

questions.prompt: A team trained a review-classification model using a tokenizer that splits text into subword pieces. Months later, an engineer swaps the production service to a whole-word tokenizer to save time. No errors are logged. What is the most likely result?
choices: The model receives tokens it never learned, and accuracy quietly drops
The service crashes immediately, because the model rejects unknown tokens
The model runs faster and accuracy stays the same, because tokens are just text
Accuracy improves, because whole words carry more meaning than subwords
questions.why: Production must tokenize exactly as training did; otherwise the model gets tokens it never learned, and performance degrades silently rather than failing loudly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how TF-IDF and word embeddings each turn text into numbers, when you would pick each, and name one limit of TF-IDF.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both start after tokenization, which splits text into tokens such as words or subwords. TF-IDF gives each word in a document a score. It multiplies how often the word appears in that document by how rare the word is across all documents. Words like "the" score near zero, and distinctive words like "refund" score high. It is cheap, needs no training, and is easy to explain, so it suits keyword search or a quick document classifier. Its limit is that it treats every word as unrelated and ignores order. "Car" and "automobile" look different, and "not good" looks like "good". Word embeddings are learned vectors that place words used in similar contexts near each other, so they capture meaning and synonyms. That helps sentiment analysis, NER, and text generation. The tradeoff is that embeddings need training data and compute, and they are harder to interpret.
rubricPoints: Says tokenization splits text into tokens before any numeric representation is built.
Explains TF-IDF as frequency in one document times rarity across all documents.
Explains embeddings as learned vectors where similar words sit close together.
Names a TF-IDF limit such as ignoring word order or synonyms.
Matches each method to a fitting use or tradeoff, such as cost and interpretability versus capturing meaning.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests picking the right NLP technique for a described scenario, such as sentiment analysis versus NER versus topic modeling, and no current mission or planned engine practices text processing, so reasoning through exam-style situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: Computer vision is the part of data science that teaches software to make sense of images and video. Three ideas come up again and again. Optical character recognition turns pictures of text, like a scanned receipt, into text a computer can search. Object detection finds things in an image and draws a box around each one. Tracking follows those same things from frame to frame in a video. Data augmentation makes extra training pictures by flipping, rotating or brightening the ones you already have. It is like a teacher showing the same flashcard from different angles so the student learns the idea, not the card.
lessons.guessPrompt: A parking garage camera records video of cars coming in. It needs to count each car once and read its license plate. Which jobs do you think software must do here, and in what order?
lessons.teach:
Computer vision (CV) means models that take pixels as input and produce useful output. Three techniques matter here.

Optical character recognition (OCR) converts images of printed or handwritten characters into machine-readable text. It usually finds the regions that contain text, then recognizes the characters or words inside them. Choose it when the problem is reading what is written, such as invoices, forms or license plates.

Object detection answers two questions: what is in the image, and where is it? It outputs bounding boxes. A bounding box is a rectangle given by coordinates. Each box comes with a class label, such as car or person, and a confidence score, which is how sure the model is. This differs from image classification, which gives one label for the whole image. Object tracking extends detection to video. It links detections across frames and gives each object a persistent ID.

Data augmentation creates altered copies of training images, using flips, rotations, crops, brightness changes or added noise. You get more variety without collecting new data. It works because a small change should not change the label: a cat flipped left to right is still a cat. This reduces overfitting, which is when a model memorizes the training set instead of learning general patterns.

Worked example: a garage bills cars automatically. Step 1: detection boxes each car in every frame. Step 2: tracking gives one car the ID 17, so it is counted once, not thirty times per second. Step 3: OCR reads the plate inside that box. Step 4: night footage is scarce, so augmentation adds darkened, noisy copies of the training images.

Common mistake: augmenting in ways that change the meaning. Mirroring text produces shapes that are not real characters, and rotating a 6 halfway around makes a 9. Augment training data only, never the test set. In production, missing tracking causes double billing, and careless augmentation makes OCR misread plates.

questions.prompt: A city archive wants to turn 4,000 scanned handwritten building permits into searchable text. It has only 300 labelled permit scans to train on. The plan so far: Step 1, the model finds the regions of each scan that contain handwriting. Step 2, it recognizes the characters and words inside those regions and outputs machine-readable text. Step 3, because 300 scans is too few and the model starts memorizing them, the team uses data augmentation. Step 4 is missing. Which choice correctly describes how they should augment?
choices: Mirror every training scan left to right, because doubling the number of images is what matters most
Rotate training scans halfway around (180 degrees) so the model learns to read pages placed upside down
Make copies of the training scans only, with small rotations, slight brightness changes and a little added noise
Apply the same random changes to the training scans and the test scans so both sets look alike
questions.why: Small rotations, brightness changes and noise keep each character's meaning while adding variety, and augmentation belongs on training data only, never the test set.

questions.prompt: An energy company flies drones over a solar farm. For each photo, engineers need to know which panels are cracked and exactly where each cracked panel sits in the image, so a crew can find it. Which computer-vision technique fits this problem?
choices: Object detection, which outputs a bounding box, a class label and a confidence score for each panel
Image classification, which gives one label such as 'cracked' or 'fine' for the whole photo
Data augmentation, which creates altered copies of the drone photos
Optical character recognition, which reads the serial numbers printed on the panels
questions.why: The problem asks both what is in the image and where it is, which is what object detection answers with labelled bounding boxes.

questions.prompt: A concert venue runs a model on its entrance camera video at 25 frames per second to count visitors. The model correctly draws a box around each person in every frame, but the nightly total is roughly 25 times the number of tickets sold. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The model needs data augmentation because the training images were too few
The system should use image classification instead of boxes
The confidence scores are too high, so extra boxes are being drawn
Detections are not linked across frames, so there is no object tracking giving each person one persistent ID
questions.why: Without tracking, the same person detected in each frame is counted again, so one visitor becomes many counts.

questions.prompt: A bank is training a model to read handwritten amounts on cheques. A data scientist proposes several augmentations for the training images. Which one is most likely to harm the model?
choices: Slightly raising or lowering the brightness
Adding a small amount of random noise
Cropping a few pixels from the image edges
Rotating some digit images 180 degrees
questions.why: Turning a digit halfway around can change its meaning, such as a 6 becoming a 9, so the label no longer matches the image.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how OCR, object detection, tracking and data augmentation differ, and when you would pick each one. Name one limit or tradeoff, such as when augmentation can backfire.
lessons.modelAnswer: OCR turns images of text into actual text. I would use it when the task is reading something, like a form or a plate. Object detection finds objects in a single image and returns a box, a label and a confidence score for each one. Classification only gives one label for the whole picture. Tracking adds time. It links detections across video frames and keeps an ID on each object, so you can count or follow it without double counting. Data augmentation is a training trick, not an output. You make flipped, rotated or relit copies of training images so the model generalizes and overfits less. The tradeoff is that every transformation must keep the label true. Mirroring text or rotating a 6 into a 9 teaches the model wrong answers. Also, augment only the training data, never the test set.
rubricPoints: OCR converts images of text into machine-readable text.
Object detection returns bounding boxes with class labels and confidence scores, unlike whole-image classification.
Tracking links detections across video frames with persistent IDs, which prevents double counting.
Data augmentation creates modified training images to add variety and reduce overfitting.
Augmentations must preserve the label and apply to training data only.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers computer vision, and the exam skill is matching a described scenario to the right technique, which is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style situations.

lessons.plain: These are four specialist toolkits, each built for a particular shape of problem. Graph analysis studies connections, like who knows whom in a network. Reinforcement learning teaches a program to make a series of choices by trial and error, earning points for good outcomes. Fraud and anomaly detection hunts for the rare record that does not fit the normal pattern. Signal processing cleans up and reads data that flows over time, like sound or sensor readings. Think of a hospital with specialists. You would not send a broken arm to the eye doctor. The skill here is matching each problem to the right specialist rather than just saying 'use AI'.
lessons.guessPrompt: A delivery company wants software that learns, by trying different route choices day after day and seeing which ones lead to faster deliveries, how to pick better routes over time. Which of the four (graph analysis, reinforcement learning, anomaly detection, signal processing) do you guess fits best, and why?
lessons.teach:
Each of these four techniques is matched to a specific shape of problem.

Graph analysis works on data stored as a graph. Nodes are things, such as people or accounts. Edges are relationships between them, such as 'sent money to'. Graph analysis answers questions about connections. Centrality measures how important or well-connected a node is. Community detection finds tightly linked groups. Shortest path finds the fewest hops between two nodes.

Reinforcement learning (RL) trains an agent, which is a decision-maker. The agent takes actions in an environment and receives a reward, a score signal. Over time it learns a policy, a rule for choosing actions, that maximizes total reward. RL fits a series of decisions where no labeled 'correct answer' exists, such as robot control or game play.

Fraud and anomaly detection finds anomalies, also called outliers: records that differ sharply from normal behavior. Fraud is rare and confirmed labels are scarce. So this often uses unsupervised methods, which need no labels. One example is the isolation forest, which spots unusual points because random splits separate them quickly.

Signal processing handles data measured over time or space, such as audio, vibration or sensor readings. It filters out noise and uses transforms. The Fourier transform, for example, rewrites a signal as the set of frequencies it contains.

Worked example: a card makes 40 small purchases in ten minutes across five countries.
Step 1: the task is spotting rare, unusual behavior, so this is anomaly detection.
Step 2: the card normally makes two purchases a day in one city. This event falls far outside that pattern, so it scores as an outlier.
Step 3: the bank links cards that share a device and address into a graph. Community detection reveals a ring of 30 cards, which is graph analysis.
Step 4: nothing here chooses actions for a reward, so RL does not apply.

Common mistake: treating fraud as ordinary classification and judging the model by accuracy. If only 0.1 percent of transactions are fraud, a model that always says 'not fraud' is 99.9 percent accurate yet catches nothing. In a running system, losses then pass silently. So measure how many real frauds are caught, and retune thresholds as normal behavior drifts.

questions.prompt: A wind farm records vibration from 12 turbines at 1,000 readings per second. The engineers want to spot a turbine that is starting to fail. Step 1: the data is measured over time, so this is a signal-processing problem. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: turbine 7 shows a strong 90 Hz component that the other 11 turbines lack. That pattern is rare and far from normal, so it is flagged as an anomaly. Step 4: the task needs no relationships between turbines, so graph analysis is not needed. Which step belongs at Step 2?
choices: Filter out noise, then apply a Fourier transform to rewrite each signal as the frequencies it contains
Label every reading as fault or normal, then judge the model by its overall accuracy
Train a reinforcement-learning agent that earns a reward each time it slows down a turbine
Link the turbines into a graph and use centrality to find the most important turbine
questions.why: Step 3 talks about a 90 Hz frequency component, which only appears after a Fourier transform rewrites the time-based vibration signal as the set of frequencies it contains.

questions.prompt: In reinforcement learning, an agent (the decision-maker) takes actions and receives rewards (score signals). What is the agent's policy?
choices: The environment the agent acts in
The rule the agent uses to choose actions so that total reward is as high as possible
The labeled correct answer for each decision
The score the agent receives after each action
questions.why: A policy is the agent's learned rule for picking actions, shaped over time to maximize total reward.

questions.prompt: A mobile phone company stores its call records as a graph. Each subscriber is a node, and each 'called' relationship is an edge. Marketing wants the single subscriber who is best connected, to invite them to a referral campaign. Which technique fits?
choices: Shortest path, to count the fewest hops between two subscribers
Centrality, to measure how important or well connected each subscriber is
Community detection, to find tightly linked groups of subscribers
An isolation forest, to find subscribers whose calling is unusual
questions.why: Centrality scores how important or well connected a node is, which is exactly the question of which single subscriber is best connected.

questions.prompt: An insurer builds a claims-fraud model. Only 0.2 percent of claims are fraudulent. The model reports 99.8 percent accuracy, but it never flags a single claim. What is the best response?
choices: Switch to signal processing, because claims arrive over time
Raise accuracy further by adding more ordinary claims to the training data
Measure how many real frauds the model catches, because accuracy hides that it misses them all
Accept the model, because 99.8 percent accuracy shows it works well
questions.why: When fraud is this rare, a model that always says 'not fraud' scores high accuracy yet catches nothing. Counting the real frauds it catches exposes the failure before losses pass silently.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between graph analysis, reinforcement learning, anomaly detection and signal processing for a new problem, and name one limit or tradeoff of at least one of them.
lessons.modelAnswer: I look at the shape of the problem first. If the question is about relationships, such as who is connected to whom, influential nodes or hidden groups, I use graph analysis. If a system must make a sequence of decisions and learn from rewards rather than labeled answers, that is reinforcement learning. If I need to find rare records that break the normal pattern, like fraud, I use anomaly detection, often unsupervised because labels are scarce. If the data is a signal over time, such as audio or sensor readings, I use signal processing to filter noise and examine frequencies, for example with a Fourier transform. One tradeoff is that anomaly detection flags anything unusual, not only fraud. Thresholds trade missed fraud against false alarms, and accuracy is misleading when fraud is rare. Another limit is that RL needs many trials, which can be costly or unsafe in the real world.
rubricPoints: Graph analysis is for relationship data of nodes and edges, using ideas like centrality and community detection.
Reinforcement learning has an agent learn a policy from rewards over a sequence of actions, without labeled answers.
Anomaly detection finds rare outliers, often with unsupervised methods, because fraud labels are scarce.
Signal processing filters and transforms time or sensor data, for example into frequencies.
Names a real limit, such as accuracy being misleading on rare fraud, false-alarm thresholds, or RL needing many costly trials.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is reading a scenario and naming the right specialized technique, so reasoning through short exam-style situations adds the most, and no current mission or planned engine practices these methods.

scenarios.title: Lumen Parcel Co.: Checking a Damage-Detection Model and Choosing the Right Tests
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Lumen Parcel Co., a fictional delivery company, as a junior data analyst. The operations team uses a classifier, which is a model that sorts each item into one of two groups. Here it labels every parcel photo as either damaged or not damaged, so staff can pull damaged parcels before they reach customers. Your manager asks you to check the model and help plan two studies.

A few terms first. A confusion matrix is a small table that counts how a classifier's guesses line up with the truth. A true positive (TP) is a damaged parcel the model correctly flagged. A false positive (FP) is a good parcel the model wrongly flagged. A false negative (FN) is a damaged parcel the model missed. A true negative (TN) is a good parcel correctly left alone. Accuracy is the share of all guesses that were right, (TP + TN) divided by the total. Precision answers the question 'of the parcels we flagged, how many were really damaged?' and equals TP / (TP + FP). Recall answers 'of the parcels that were really damaged, how many did we catch?' and equals TP / (TP + FN). The F1 score blends the two into one number using the harmonic mean, a kind of average that is pulled down hard by whichever value is lower: F1 = 2 x precision x recall / (precision + recall). A common mistake is to trust accuracy alone when one group is rare. If only a few parcels are damaged, a model that flags nothing at all still looks highly accurate while catching zero damage.

Last month the model checked 1,000 parcels at the main warehouse, and 50 of them were truly damaged. The model flagged 60 parcels. Of those 60, 40 were truly damaged (TP = 40) and 20 were fine (FP = 20). It missed 10 damaged parcels (FN = 10), and it correctly passed 930 good parcels (TN = 930).

Bayes' rule is a formula for updating a probability when you learn new evidence. For this model it reads: P(damaged given flagged) = P(flagged given damaged) x P(damaged) / P(flagged). P(flagged given damaged) is the recall. P(damaged) is the base rate, meaning how common damage is before you look at any model output. P(flagged) is the overall chance of a flag, which is recall x base rate + false positive rate x (1 - base rate). The false positive rate is the share of good parcels that get flagged, FP / (FP + TN). The key idea is that when the base rate is small, even a decent model produces many flags that turn out to be wrong, because good parcels vastly outnumber damaged ones. The running consequence is that staff can lose trust in the alerts and start ignoring them.

Finally, some testing vocabulary. A hypothesis test is a structured way to decide whether a pattern in data is likely real or just chance. It starts from a null hypothesis, which is the 'nothing is going on' claim, such as 'there is no difference between groups'. The test produces a p-value, the probability of seeing results at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. A small p-value, commonly below 0.05, leads you to reject the null. A t-test compares the averages (means) of a numeric measurement between exactly two groups. ANOVA (analysis of variance) compares the means of a numeric measurement across three or more groups in one test. Running many separate t-tests instead inflates the chance of a false alarm. A chi-squared test checks whether two categorical variables, meaning variables that sort items into named groups rather than measuring a number, are related. It works by comparing the counts you observed in each combination with the counts you would expect if the variables were unrelated.

Your tasks:
1. Using the confusion matrix above, calculate accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for the main warehouse. Explain in one or two sentences why accuracy alone gives a misleading picture here.
2. Show that Bayes' rule gives the same chance that a flagged parcel is truly damaged as the precision you found. Then a new rural warehouse will use the same model, with the same recall and false positive rate, but only 1% of its parcels are damaged. Use Bayes' rule to estimate the chance that a flagged parcel there is truly damaged, and state what this means for staff.
3. The team wants two studies. Study A asks whether average delivery time in hours differs across the company's three regional hubs. Study B asks whether damage (damaged or not damaged) is related to packaging type (box, padded envelope or tube). For each study, name the correct test, say why it fits, and write the null hypothesis in plain words.
subParts: Confusion-matrix metrics and why accuracy misleads
Bayes' rule and the effect of a lower base rate
Choosing ANOVA versus chi-squared and stating null hypotheses
modelAnswer: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / total = (40 + 930) / 1,000 = 970 / 1,000 = 0.97, or 97%. Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 40 / 60 = about 0.667, or 66.7%. Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 40 / 50 = 0.80, or 80%. F1 = 2 x 0.667 x 0.80 / (0.667 + 0.80) = 1.067 / 1.467 = about 0.727. Accuracy misleads because damaged parcels are rare (5%). A model that flagged nothing would still score 950 / 1,000 = 95% accuracy while catching no damage. Precision, recall and F1 show the real trade-off: one in three flags is a false alarm, and one in five damaged parcels is missed. Full credit needs all four values, which may be rounded, plus the rare-class explanation.

Main warehouse: base rate = 50 / 1,000 = 0.05. Recall = 0.80. False positive rate = FP / (FP + TN) = 20 / 950 = about 0.0211. P(flagged) = 0.80 x 0.05 + 0.0211 x 0.95 = 0.04 + 0.02 = 0.06. P(damaged given flagged) = 0.04 / 0.06 = about 0.667. This matches the precision of 66.7%, which also matches the 60 flags out of 1,000 parcels. Rural warehouse: base rate = 0.01. P(flagged) = 0.80 x 0.01 + 0.0211 x 0.99 = 0.008 + 0.0208 = about 0.0288. P(damaged given flagged) = 0.008 / 0.0288 = about 0.28, or roughly 28%. Meaning: even though the model itself is unchanged, about 7 in 10 flags at the rural site would be false alarms, because good parcels so heavily outnumber damaged ones. Staff should expect many wrong flags and do a quick manual check. The team should not assume the main-site precision carries over, and should watch for staff starting to ignore alerts. Accept answers between 27% and 28%.

Study A: use ANOVA. Delivery time is a numeric measurement, and we are comparing its average across three groups (the hubs). ANOVA compares three or more means in one test, while a t-test handles only two groups, and running several t-tests would raise the false-alarm risk. Null hypothesis: the average delivery time is the same at all three hubs. Study B: use a chi-squared test. Both damage status and packaging type are categorical, so the data are counts in each combination, not averages. The chi-squared test compares the observed counts with the counts expected if the two variables were unrelated. Null hypothesis: damage status is not related to packaging type, meaning the chance of damage is the same for boxes, padded envelopes and tubes. Credit requires the correct test for each study, a reason tied to the data type (numeric versus categorical) and the number of groups, and a correctly worded null hypothesis for each.

scenarios.title: Choosing and Explaining a Rental Forecast Model at Harborline Bikes
scenarios.scenario:
Harborline Bikes is a fictional bike-sharing company in a coastal city. You are a junior data analyst on a small team building a model that predicts how many bikes will be rented each day, so operations staff can decide how many bikes to move between stations each night.

Your dataset has one row per day for three years. Its columns are: daily rentals (a count), average temperature (a number), humidity (a number), wind speed (a number), and weather type (a category with the values clear, cloudy, rain, and snow).

Step one. Before any modeling, your lead asks you to do exploratory data analysis (EDA), which means looking at the data with summaries and charts to understand it before building anything. She wants three charts. The first shows how temperature relates to daily rentals. The second compares the spread of daily rentals across the four weather types. The third shows, in one view, how strongly every pair of numeric columns moves together.

Step two. The team fits a first model, a simple linear regression, which predicts rentals as a straight-line combination of the inputs. You check its residuals. A residual is the actual value minus the predicted value for one day. On a residuals-versus-predicted plot, the dots form a clear U shape instead of a flat, even band around zero. On a Q-Q plot (quantile-quantile plot, which compares the residuals against a perfect bell-shaped normal distribution), the points bend away from the straight reference line at both ends.

Step three. The team tests more models and records every run in an experiment tracker, a log of each model's settings and scores. The business requirements are: (a) the model must answer in under 200 milliseconds, because it runs inside a nightly planning tool with a time limit; and (b) its error must be at least 25% lower than the benchmark. The benchmark is a seasonal naive forecast, a deliberately simple method that predicts today's rentals as the count from the same weekday last week. Error is measured as MAE (mean absolute error, the average size of a miss in bikes, ignoring whether the miss was too high or too low). Results on the same held-out test data, meaning days the models never saw while training: Seasonal naive benchmark: MAE 70 bikes. Model A, a large gradient-boosted tree ensemble: MAE 41 bikes, response time 900 ms. Model B, a smaller random forest: MAE 44 bikes, response time 60 ms. Model C, the original linear regression: MAE 58 bikes, response time 5 ms.

Step four. A colleague drafts a bar chart for the executive team comparing the MAE of the benchmark and Model B. The vertical axis starts at 40 instead of 0, so Model B's bar looks about ten times shorter than the benchmark's bar. The bars are told apart only by red versus green, and the chart has no title or labels explaining what MAE means.

Your tasks:
1. For each of the three EDA charts in step one, name the chart type you would use and say why it fits the data types involved.
2. Interpret the two diagnostic plots in step two. What does each pattern tell you about the linear model, and what is one reasonable next step?
3. Using the results in step three, recommend one model. Show how you checked each requirement against each model.
4. Name the problems with the colleague's executive chart in step four, explain why each one matters, and describe how you would fix it for that audience.
subParts: Pick EDA charts by data type
modelAnswer:
Temperature versus rentals: use a scatter plot. Both columns are numeric, and a scatter plot puts one on each axis with a dot per day. That makes the shape of the relationship visible, including whether it curves, for example rentals rising with warmth and then falling in extreme heat.

Rentals by weather type: use a box-and-whisker plot (box plot) with one box per category. This pairs a categorical column with a numeric one. Each box shows the median, the middle 50% of days, the overall range, and outliers, so you can compare both the typical value and the spread across clear, cloudy, rain, and snow days.

All numeric pairs at once: use a heat map of the correlation matrix. A correlation matrix is a table of correlation values for every pair of numeric columns. The heat map colors each cell by how strongly that pair moves together, so strong relationships, such as temperature with rentals, stand out in one view.

This is multivariate analysis, meaning several variables are examined together, as opposed to univariate analysis of one column at a time. A common mistake is using a scatter plot for the weather category, which piles the dots into four overlapping columns that are hard to read.

U-shaped residuals versus predicted values: the errors are not random. The model is systematically wrong in one direction at the low and high ends and in the other direction in the middle. That is the signature of non-linearity: the true relationship curves, but a straight-line model cannot bend to follow it. A good model leaves a flat, patternless band of residuals around zero.

Q-Q plot bending away at both ends: the residuals have heavier tails than a normal distribution. In other words, there are more large misses than a well-fitting linear model should produce. This is partly a side effect of the missed curve, and it means confidence intervals and significance tests from this linear model are not trustworthy.

Reasonable next steps (any one is acceptable): add non-linear terms, such as temperature squared, or transform the target, such as taking the log of rentals. Alternatively, move to a model that can capture curves on its own, such as a tree-based model. Then re-check both plots. If you ignore these patterns, the model would consistently under- or over-supply bikes on the hottest, coldest, and busiest days, which are exactly the days when planning errors hurt most.

Recommend Model B, the random forest.

Requirement (b), error at least 25% better than the benchmark: 25% of 70 is 17.5, so the maximum allowed MAE is 70 minus 17.5, which is 52.5 bikes. Model A at 41 passes. Model B at 44 passes. Model C at 58 fails.

Requirement (a), response time under 200 ms: Model A at 900 ms fails. Model B at 60 ms passes. Model C at 5 ms passes.

Only Model B passes both requirements. Model A has the best MAE, but it breaks a hard design constraint. Choosing it would make the nightly planning tool run past its time limit, and good accuracy is useless if the result arrives too late.

This is requirements validation: checking each candidate against the stated business needs, not just picking the top score. Benchmarking against the seasonal naive method proves the model adds real value beyond a trivial rule. The comparison is fair because every model was scored on the same held-out test data. The common mistake here is recommending Model A simply because it has the lowest error.

Problem 1, truncated vertical axis starting at 40: bar length should be proportional to the value. Cutting the axis exaggerates the gap, making the improvement look roughly ten times larger instead of about 37% (from 70 down to 44). This is deceptive charting, and executives could set unrealistic expectations or lose trust when they learn the real numbers. Fix: start the bar axis at 0.

Problem 2, red versus green as the only difference: people with red-green color vision deficiency may not be able to tell the bars apart, so the chart fails accessibility. Fix: label each bar directly with its name and value. Use a colorblind-safe palette, or add patterns, so color is never the only cue.

Problem 3, no title, labels, or plain explanation: an executive audience needs the business meaning, not the jargon. Fix: give the chart a clear headline, such as 'New forecast misses by about 44 bikes a day, versus 70 today.' Label the axis in plain words, such as 'average daily forecast error (bikes).' Add one sentence on what this means for operations.

For executives, keep the chart to one simple, honest comparison with the key takeaway stated outright. Save detailed diagnostics like residual and Q-Q plots for peer or technical audiences.

scenarios.title: Catching Rare Fraud at Harbourline Payments
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined the data team at Harbourline Payments, a fictional company that processes card payments for small shops. Your lead, Priya, hands you a project: build a model that flags fraudulent transactions. The data has 200,000 past transactions, and each one is labelled either fraud or not fraud. Only 400 of them, which is 0.2 percent, are fraud.

A few terms first. Class imbalance means one label (a class) is far rarer than the other, as fraud is here. Accuracy is the share of all predictions that are correct. Recall is the share of real fraud cases the model actually catches. Oversampling is a fix for imbalance: you add more copies of the rare class to the training data. SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) is a smarter kind of oversampling. Instead of copying rows exactly, it makes new, slightly different fraud examples by blending a fraud row with one of its nearby fraud neighbours.

A decision tree is a model that predicts by asking a chain of yes-or-no questions about the data, such as 'Is the amount over 500?'. Overfitting means a model has memorised the quirks of its training data, so it scores well there but poorly on new data. That kind of error is called high variance, meaning the model's predictions swing a lot depending on which data it was trained on. High bias is the opposite problem: a model too simple to capture the real pattern. The bias-variance tradeoff is the balance between these two errors.

Bootstrap aggregation, usually called bagging, trains many models, each on a random sample of rows drawn with replacement (so some rows repeat), and then combines their votes. A random forest is bagging applied to decision trees, with one extra twist: each tree also considers only a random subset of the columns at each split. Averaging many varied trees cancels out much of their individual noise, which lowers variance. Boosting, as in XGBoost, works differently. It builds trees one after another, and each new tree focuses on fixing the errors the previous trees made. That mainly reduces bias. Both bagging and boosting are ensemble models, meaning they combine many models into one.

Cross-validation is a way to test a model honestly. In k-fold cross-validation you split the data into k equal parts called folds. You train on k minus 1 folds, test on the one left out, and repeat until every fold has been the test fold once. Stratified folds keep the same fraud percentage in every fold. Data leakage happens when information from the test data sneaks into training, which makes scores look better than they really are.

Model drift is when a deployed model's performance gets worse over time because real-world data stops looking like the training data, for example when fraudsters change their tactics.

A colleague has already tried something. He trained a single, very deep decision tree on the raw data and reported 99.8 percent accuracy on the training data. On held-out data, however, it caught almost no fraud. He also plans to run SMOTE on the full dataset first and then do cross-validation.

1. Explain why 99.8 percent accuracy is misleading here, and name a specific technique from this scenario to address the class imbalance.
2. The single deep tree does great on training data but badly on new data. Name the type of error, and choose a specific tree-based ensemble to reduce it. Say why that ensemble works.
3. Describe how to cross-validate correctly, and explain what is wrong with the colleague's plan to run SMOTE before splitting.
4. Six months after launch, recall falls from 80 percent to 55 percent, even though nobody changed the model. Name what is happening and say what the team should do.
modelAnswer: Only 0.2 percent of transactions are fraud. A model that labels every single transaction as not fraud would therefore be right 99.8 percent of the time while catching zero fraud. Accuracy hides the failure on the rare class, so the team should judge the model by recall on fraud instead. To fix the class imbalance, use SMOTE (or plain oversampling) on the training data. SMOTE creates new synthetic fraud examples by blending existing fraud rows with their nearby fraud neighbours. This gives the model enough fraud cases to learn the pattern, rather than simply learning to always say not fraud.

This is overfitting, which is high variance: the deep tree memorised quirks of the training data. A good choice is a random forest, which is bagging applied to decision trees. Each tree is trained on a random sample of rows drawn with replacement, and each split looks at only a random subset of columns, so the trees end up different from one another. Combining their votes cancels out much of each tree's individual noise, and that lowers variance. Boosting (XGBoost) mainly targets bias, so it is not the first answer for a model whose problem is high variance. Stating 'train a better model' without naming random forest or bagging is not sufficient.

Use stratified k-fold cross-validation. Split the data into k folds that each keep the same fraud percentage. Train on k minus 1 folds and test on the remaining fold, repeating until every fold has been the test fold once, then average the results, for example the recall. Apply SMOTE inside each round, to the training folds only, and leave the test fold untouched. The colleague's plan causes data leakage. Running SMOTE on the full dataset first creates synthetic fraud rows blended from neighbours that may later land in the test fold, so the model is tested on near-copies of what it trained on. The scores will look better than real-world performance.

This is model drift. Real-world data, such as new fraud tactics, no longer looks like the training data, so performance drops even though the model itself is unchanged. The team should keep monitoring recall in production, retrain the model on recent labelled transactions (applying the same SMOTE and stratified cross-validation process), and redeploy it. Ideally they should also set an alert threshold so that future drops trigger retraining early.

scenarios.title: Freshline Grocers: Fixing a Demand-Forecast Workflow
scenarios.scenario:
