Freshline Grocers is a fictional regional supermarket chain. Its three-person data team built a demand-forecasting model, a program that predicts how many units of each product every store will sell tomorrow, so stores can order the right amount of fresh food. The business judges the project with a KPI (key performance indicator, a number the business tracks to decide whether something is working): forecast error, measured as MAE (mean absolute error, the average size of the gap between predicted and actual sales, ignoring whether the guess was too high or too low). You have just joined the team, and your manager asks you to review four problems.

Problem A. Sales records come from the till system with timestamps in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time, the single world reference clock), written like 2024-03-06T02:30:00Z. Weather records come from a supplier in each store's local time, written like 03/05/2024 9:30 PM. The team merges (joins row by row on a shared key) the two tables on the date text alone. A sale at 02:30 UTC on 6 March, which was 9:30 PM on 5 March in the store's Eastern time zone, is being matched to 6 March weather.

Problem B. One store's daily sales for bananas usually sit between 300 and 1,100 units, but one day shows 40,000 because a clerk typed extra zeros. That single value is pulling the model's predictions upward for every store. The team does not want to delete the row, because the day itself was real and other columns on it are correct.

Problem C. Two analysts edit the same notebook file (a document that mixes code and results) on a shared drive. Files are named things like forecast_final_v3_REALLY_final. Last week one analyst's changes overwrote the other's, and nobody can rebuild the exact model that was running last month, or say who changed what.

Problem D. The model was deployed (put into live use so stores receive its forecasts) eight weeks ago. Two weeks after launch, Freshline opened a new small-format city store type with very different shopping habits. Store managers only complained this week that orders were badly off. Nobody on the team was watching how the model performed after launch.

Reference notes the team keeps on its wiki. Date/time standardization means converting every timestamp to one agreed format and one time zone, commonly ISO 8601 (an international layout such as 2024-03-05T21:30:00) stored in UTC, before combining datasets. Winsorization means capping extreme values: you pick a low and a high percentile (a percentile is the value below which that percentage of the data falls, so the 99th percentile is higher than 99 percent of values) and replace anything beyond those limits with the limit value itself, keeping the row. Version control means using a tool such as Git that records every change to code as a saved snapshot with an author, a time and a message, lets people work on separate branches (parallel copies) and merge them, and lets you return to any earlier snapshot. Performance monitoring means continuously tracking a deployed model's live results, such as its MAE, against the level it achieved at launch, with an alert when it crosses a set threshold, so the team can investigate and retrain. Parquet is a columnar file format (it stores data column by column, which compresses well and speeds up reading only the columns you need). CI/CD (continuous integration and continuous delivery) is automation that tests and releases code every time it changes. CRISP-DM (Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining) is a six-phase workflow model running from business understanding to deployment. Synthetic data is artificially generated data that imitates real data's patterns. Container orchestration, for example Kubernetes, is software that starts, scales and restarts packaged applications across many machines.

For each problem, name the one specific practice from the reference notes that addresses it, explain why it fits, and apply it to the example given.

1. Problem A: name the missing practice and show how the 02:30 UTC sale should be handled before the merge.
2. Problem B: name the missing practice and show what happens to the 40,000 value if the team caps at the 1st and 99th percentiles and the 99th percentile is 1,150.
3. Problem C: name the missing practice and explain how it would have prevented both the overwrite and the inability to rebuild last month's model.
4. Problem D: name the missing practice and explain how it would have caught the new-store problem earlier, including what it would compare and what happens when an alert fires.
modelAnswer: The missing practice is date/time standardization. The two sources use different formats and different time zones, so joining on the date text puts some sales on the wrong day. Fix: before merging, convert every timestamp to one format (ISO 8601) and one time zone (UTC is the common choice). Trace: the weather reading 03/05/2024 9:30 PM Eastern is parsed as a real date and time, then shifted by the Eastern offset (UTC minus 5 hours in early March) to 2024-03-06T02:30:00 UTC. The sale is already 2024-03-06T02:30:00 UTC, so the two rows now line up on the same instant. If the business wants daily totals by the store's own calendar day, the team converts both to local time consistently instead; the key point is that both sides use the same rule. A common mistake is reformatting the text so it looks alike without converting the time zone, which leaves the evening-sale mismatch in place. Consequence if ignored: the model learns from wrong weather for late-day sales, which raises forecast error.

The missing practice is winsorization. It fits because the team wants to stop one extreme value from distorting the model without deleting the row, and winsorization keeps the row but caps the value. Trace: set limits at the 1st and 99th percentiles. The 99th percentile is 1,150, and 40,000 is above it, so 40,000 is replaced with 1,150. Normal values between the two limits, such as 300 to 1,100, stay unchanged, and any value below the 1st percentile would be raised to that limit. The row, its date and its other correct columns remain in the data. A common mistake is confusing it with deleting outliers (trimming), which loses the real day, or capping so tightly that genuine busy days are flattened. Consequence: predictions are no longer pulled upward for every store by one typing error.

The missing practice is version control (for example Git). It fits because the problem is uncontrolled edits to shared code with no history. Each analyst works on their own branch, saves changes as snapshots with an author, time and message, and merges branches back together; when both changed the same lines, the tool flags a conflict to resolve instead of silently overwriting, which prevents last week's loss. Because every snapshot is kept, the team can return to the exact code version used for last month's model (ideally tagged at deployment) and rebuild it, and the history shows who changed what and why. Filenames like final_v3_REALLY_final become unnecessary. A common mistake is thinking a shared drive or file-copy naming counts as version control; it has no reliable history or merge. Consequence if ignored: the team cannot reproduce or roll back a live model when it misbehaves.

The missing practice is performance monitoring of the deployed model. It fits because the model was launched and then not watched, so a change in real-world conditions went unnoticed for weeks. The team would record the model's MAE at launch as a baseline, then calculate live MAE regularly (for example daily) by comparing forecasts with actual sales, ideally broken down by store type. They set an alert threshold, such as live MAE more than 20 percent above baseline. When the new small-format stores opened, their error would have risen within days, crossed the threshold and triggered an alert. On an alert, the team investigates the cause (here, shopping patterns the model never learned) and retrains or adjusts the model with data from the new stores, then keeps monitoring. A common mistake is checking accuracy only once before launch and assuming it stays the same. Consequence if ignored: months of bad orders, wasted fresh food or empty shelves, and a worsening KPI that nobody sees until managers complain.

scenarios.title: Picking the Right Technique at Larkspur Market
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Market is a fictional regional grocery chain with 40 stores and an online ordering site. You have just joined its small data team, and your manager, Dana, has a backlog of four requests from different departments. Each department has asked for 'some AI'. Dana wants you to name the specific technique that fits each request and explain why in a sentence or two, so she can plan the work.

The marketing team has three new homepage banners. They want to learn which one gets the most clicks, but they don't want to waste weeks showing a weak banner to a third of all visitors. They would like the system to shift traffic toward the better banner while it is still learning.

The delivery team plans next week's van schedules. They want the lowest total fuel cost, but each van can carry at most 60 crates, every driver's shift ends after 8 hours, and every order must be delivered.

The customer service team receives about 2,000 free-text complaint emails a week. They want two things: a label on each email saying whether the customer is happy, neutral, or angry, and an automatic pull-out of specific names mentioned in the text, such as product brands and store towns, so they can see which stores and brands come up most.

The finance team still gets paper supplier invoices, which are scanned into image files. Staff retype the totals and invoice numbers by hand. Separately, a pilot project wants a camera model that finds empty shelf gaps in photos, but the team has only 300 labeled shelf photos, all taken in bright daytime light.

1. Name the technique that fits the marketing banner request and explain why it suits this situation better than a fixed split of traffic.
2. Classify the delivery problem as constrained or unconstrained optimization, and identify the goal and the limits in it.
3. Name the two natural language processing (NLP) applications the customer service team needs, meaning techniques that let a computer work with human-written text, and say what each one produces.
4. Name the computer vision technique for the invoices, and name the technique that helps the shelf-gap model cope with only 300 bright daytime photos. Describe one risk if that second technique is skipped.
modelAnswer:
This is a multi-armed bandit problem. The name comes from a gambler choosing between several slot machines, or 'one-armed bandits', each with an unknown payout. The system has to balance exploration, which means trying each banner enough to learn how well it does, against exploitation, which means showing the banner that currently looks best.

A fixed split, such as a classic A/B test, keeps showing every banner equally until the test ends. A bandit approach instead updates as clicks come in and steadily sends more visitors to the banner that is winning. That means fewer visitors see a weak banner while the team is still learning, which is exactly what marketing asked for.

Worked trace: after the first day, banner B has the highest click rate, so the bandit raises B's share of traffic. It still shows A and C now and then, in case early results were luck.

Common mistake: exploiting too early, meaning sending all traffic to the first-day leader. If that leader was only lucky, the system can get stuck on a worse banner.

This is constrained optimization. Optimization means searching for the choice that gives the best value of a goal, called the objective. It is constrained because the allowed solutions must obey hard limits, called constraints. In unconstrained optimization, any value of the decision variables would be allowed.

The objective here is to minimize total fuel cost. The constraints are that each van carries at most 60 crates, each driver's shift lasts at most 8 hours, and every order must be delivered.

Common mistake: treating the problem as unconstrained and simply minimizing fuel. The cheapest-looking 'solution' could be to deliver fewer orders or overload vans. That plan would be infeasible, meaning it breaks a rule, and it would fail in real operations.

The first application is sentiment analysis. This technique assigns each piece of text an opinion or emotion label, here happy, neutral, or angry. It produces one label, sometimes with a score, for each email.

The second is named entity recognition (NER). NER finds specific named things in text and tags each one with its type. Here it would tag product brands and store towns. It produces a list of extracted entities per email, which can then be counted to show which stores and brands appear most often.

Both usually start with tokenization, which splits raw text into smaller units called tokens, such as words, so a model can process them.

Common mistake: answering 'topic modeling' for the brand and store request. Topic modeling finds broad themes across many documents, for example 'delivery delays'. It does not reliably pull out exact names like a specific town.

For the invoices, the technique is optical character recognition (OCR). OCR converts the text inside an image, such as a scanned invoice, into machine-readable characters. The totals and invoice numbers can then be extracted automatically instead of retyped by hand.

For the shelf-gap model, the technique is data augmentation. Data augmentation creates extra training examples by making realistic changes to existing images. Examples include darkening or brightening a photo, slightly rotating or cropping it, flipping it, or adding noise. This makes the 300 photos act like a larger and more varied set, including dimmer conditions.

Risk if augmentation is skipped: the model learns only from bright daytime photos and overfits, meaning it fits the training examples too closely and generalizes poorly. In a real store at night or under weaker lighting, it would likely miss empty gaps or flag false ones. Staff could then ignore real stockouts or waste time on false alerts.
